subtopic_detail: Panic disorder pharmacotherapy initiation
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 34 year old accountant with a 4 month history of recurrent unexpected episodes of chest tightness, palpitations, hand tingling, and a sense of impending death that peak within 10 minutes and settle over 30 minutes. He now avoids the train because he had two attacks on the platform, and he telephones his wife to collect him.

He drinks 2 standard drinks on Friday evenings, has never used stimulants or cannabis, and does not use caffeine after midday. TSH, full blood count, electrolytes, ECG, and echocardiogram arranged by the emergency department 3 weeks ago were all within normal limits. He scores 16 on the PHQ-9 with no suicidal ideation and 18 on the GAD-7.

He is otherwise well, on no regular medication, has no family history of bipolar disorder, and is keen to start medication rather than commence psychological therapy at this stage.

data_table.Screening scores: PHQ-9 16 with no suicidal ideation; GAD-7 18
data_table.Prior workup: TSH, full blood count, electrolytes, ECG, echocardiogram all within normal limits
data_table.Substance use: 2 standard drinks weekly; no stimulants, no cannabis, no caffeine after midday

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 30 mg orally each evening and continue indefinitely as needed
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has evidence in depression with anxious features but is not first-line for panic disorder in eTG or RANZCP guidance; sedation and weight gain are relevant for a physically well working adult (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily and continue while panic persists
options.rationale: Regular benzodiazepine monotherapy for panic disorder carries dependence risk and blunts the exposure-based learning that resolves avoidance; short-term use is at most a bridge, not the initiating agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily and continue for symptom control
options.rationale: Beta blockers reduce sympathetic somatic symptoms in performance anxiety but do not treat the cognitive and avoidance features of panic disorder and are not recommended as monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily without any initial low-dose lead-in period
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is effective for panic disorder but starting at the standard depression dose commonly precipitates activation and worsening panic in the first fortnight; the recommendation is a lower start (5 to 10 mg) then titrate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily then increase to 50 mg after one week
options.rationale: SSRIs at low starting doses titrated up over 1 to 2 weeks are first-line pharmacotherapy for panic disorder; sertraline 25 mg titrated to 50 mg is the recommended eTG initiation regimen because full dose introduction commonly precipitates a transient jitteriness that undermines adherence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Panic Disorder CPG).

explanation.summary: Panic disorder is the DSM-5 diagnosis when recurrent unexpected panic attacks are followed by at least one month of anticipatory worry or maladaptive behavioural change. First-line pharmacotherapy in Australian practice is a low-dose SSRI titrated slowly over 1 to 2 weeks to a standard depression-range dose, because full-dose initiation commonly precipitates transient jitteriness that undermines adherence. Sertraline, escitalopram, and paroxetine all have TGA registration for panic disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy with interoceptive exposure is at least equally effective and can be run in parallel. Benzodiazepines have a limited bridging role.
key_points: SSRI titrated from low start over 1 to 2 weeks is first-line
Sertraline 25 mg then 50 mg is the eTG initiation pattern
Standard-dose SSRI start commonly precipitates activation
Benzodiazepines are not first-line monotherapy
CBT with interoceptive exposure runs alongside SSRI
explanation.pearls: Warning the patient that panic-like symptoms may transiently worsen for 1 to 2 weeks on any SSRI, and pre-prescribing 5 diazepam 5 mg tablets as a rescue, improves 12 week adherence in RANZCP audit data.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in an exclusively breastfeeding mother
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 29 year old woman 10 weeks after the birth of her first baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and describes 3 weeks of low mood, waking at 04:00 with racing thoughts, tearfulness through the day, poor appetite, and guilt about not enjoying the baby. She has no suicidal ideation and no thoughts of harming the baby. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale run by the child-health nurse today is 17 with item 10 scored zero.

She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no perinatal anxiety earlier in the pregnancy. Thyroid function, ferritin, and B12 are within normal limits. She is not taking any medications and had no antidepressant during pregnancy.

She has been attending fortnightly with the child-health nurse, has family support, and is willing to consider psychological therapy but wants to also start medication because sleep is deteriorating. She wants to continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Screening: EPDS 17 with item 10 scored zero; PHQ-9 not repeated
data_table.Baseline labs: TSH, ferritin, and B12 within normal limits
data_table.Feeding: Exclusively breastfeeding a 10 week old infant

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Advise weaning off breastfeeding before starting any antidepressant
options.rationale: Weaning is not required to treat postnatal depression pharmacologically; several SSRIs are considered safe in lactation and abrupt weaning itself worsens maternal mood (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half-life active metabolite that accumulates in neonates and gives the highest relative infant dose of the SSRIs; it is a second-line perinatal choice when the mother is already established on it, not for a new start (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

options.text: Venlafaxine 75 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has an infant relative dose higher than sertraline and lacks the same reassuring evidence base for perinatal initiation; it is reasonable if the mother was already responding to it, not first-line new (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg orally each night continued during breastfeeding
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has limited perinatal safety data and its sedation and weight gain profile are unfavourable when the mother needs to be responsive to a young infant; it is not first-line (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG).

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally each morning continued during breastfeeding
options.rationale: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because relative infant dose is under 2 percent and infant plasma levels are usually undetectable; it is the first-line perinatal antidepressant in RANZCP and eTG guidance (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression is common and treatable, and the choice of antidepressant in breastfeeding is guided by the relative infant dose (RID) of the drug in breastmilk. Sertraline consistently has the lowest RID and undetectable infant plasma levels in most studies, which is why RANZCP places it first for perinatal antidepressant initiation. Fluoxetine and citalopram have higher RID and their long-acting metabolites can accumulate in neonates; they are still reasonable if the mother was already responding to them prior to conception. Psychological therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) should be offered in parallel, and thyroid, ferritin, and B12 should be excluded as contributors before ascribing symptoms to postnatal depression.
key_points: Sertraline is first-line SSRI in breastfeeding
RID under 2 percent with undetectable infant plasma levels
Fluoxetine is not first-line new due to long half-life metabolite
Do not wean breastfeeding to start an antidepressant
Screen with EPDS and check item 10 for suicidal thoughts
explanation.pearls: The EPDS item 10 asks about thoughts of self-harm and any positive score requires same-day risk assessment even when the total score is modest; a score of 2 or 3 on item 10 with a total of 12 outweighs a total of 17 with item 10 zero.

subtopic_detail: Thiamine timing in alcohol withdrawal presenting to ED
stem:
You are the ED RMO seeing a 52 year old builder brought in by his brother because he has stopped drinking 20 hours ago after 18 years of daily heavy alcohol use averaging 20 standard drinks per day. He is diaphoretic, tremulous, mildly agitated, and confused about the date but knows his name. His CIWA-Ar score is 22.

On arrival his pulse is 118, blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg, respiratory rate is 22, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 37.6 degrees Celsius. Point-of-care glucose is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.7). Weight is 72 kg. He has no history of seizure or delirium tremens in prior withdrawals but has a lifetime pattern of poor nutrition and lost 6 kg in the last two months.

Bloods have been sent and IV access is established. The consultant asks you to co-ordinate the next steps.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 168/98 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Give IV thiamine 300 mg then IV glucose after the thiamine infusion is running
options.rationale: Parenteral thiamine before any glucose load is standard because glucose given to a thiamine deplete patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; the AU eTG dose is 300 mg IV or IM followed by ongoing daily dosing for at least 3 days (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction; RACP Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline).

options.text: Give 100 mL of 50 percent glucose IV then oral thiamine 100 mg after glucose
options.rationale: Giving concentrated glucose to a thiamine deplete patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and oral thiamine has variable absorption in malnourished heavy drinkers; the order and route are wrong (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Give oral diazepam 20 mg then reassess the CIWA-Ar score after 60 minutes
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine loading is needed for a CIWA-Ar of 22 but thiamine must be given first when point-of-care glucose is low and the patient is at high Wernicke risk; benzodiazepines alone leave the metabolic emergency unaddressed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Give haloperidol 5 mg IM to control the agitation before any other intervention
options.rationale: Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and is not first-line for alcohol withdrawal agitation; benzodiazepines are the class of choice and thiamine and glucose remain the immediate priority (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Give fixed schedule oral diazepam 10 mg six-hourly without any thiamine cover
options.rationale: A symptom-triggered regimen is preferred over a fixed schedule for uncomplicated withdrawal, and thiamine is a non-negotiable safety step in a malnourished heavy drinker regardless of the benzodiazepine strategy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal management in the ED runs on three parallel tracks: prevent Wernicke encephalopathy with parenteral thiamine before any glucose, control autonomic and neurological features with a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine schedule (usually diazepam) titrated to CIWA-Ar, and treat the metabolic and electrolyte disturbances of chronic heavy drinking. The AU thiamine dose is 300 mg IV or IM daily for at least 3 days when Wernicke risk is present, followed by oral maintenance. Giving glucose before thiamine to a thiamine-deplete patient precipitates the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. Haloperidol should be avoided as it lowers the seizure threshold in withdrawal.
key_points: Thiamine 300 mg IV or IM before any glucose load
Continue parenteral thiamine daily for at least 3 days
Symptom-triggered diazepam titrated to CIWA-Ar for withdrawal
Avoid haloperidol which lowers seizure threshold
Monitor magnesium, phosphate, and potassium
explanation.pearls: Point-of-care glucose is the trigger that catches the pre-Wernicke deteriorating patient in the ED: a value below 4 mmol/L in a heavy drinker mandates thiamine before you touch the glucose vial.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome monitoring in anorexia nervosa admission
stem:
You are the paediatric medical registrar admitting a 15 year old girl to the adolescent medical ward with restrictive anorexia nervosa. Her weight is 38 kg for a height of 165 cm, giving a BMI of 14.0. She has restricted intake to under 500 kcal per day for the last 8 weeks and lost 12 kg over that period.

On admission her pulse is 44, blood pressure is 82/48 mmHg with a postural drop of 22 mmHg systolic, respiratory rate is 14, SpO2 is 99 percent on room air, and temperature is 35.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 470 ms. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 3.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), phosphate is 0.72 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.4), magnesium is 0.72 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.0), and glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.7).

A plan has been made to start refeeding at 1000 kcal per day and increase by 200 kcal every 24 to 48 hours per the RCH eating disorders pathway. She is medically cleared for oral intake and family are supportive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 44, BP 82/48 mmHg with 22 mmHg postural drop, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Baseline biochemistry: Sodium 138 (135 to 145), potassium 3.4 (3.5 to 5.0), phosphate 0.72 (0.8 to 1.4), magnesium 0.72 (0.7 to 1.0), glucose 3.6 (3.5 to 7.7)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate monitoring plan for the first 72 hours of refeeding?

options.text: Check phosphate, magnesium, potassium and glucose daily for 5 days with intermittent cardiac observations
options.rationale: Daily bloods miss the early refeeding shift which typically peaks at 24 to 72 hours; the AU standard is 12-hourly monitoring for the first 72 hours in high-risk cases (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

options.text: Check phosphate, magnesium, potassium and glucose every 12 hours for 72 hours with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: RCH and MARSIPAN adolescent pathways mandate 12-hourly electrolyte monitoring including phosphate for the first 72 hours of refeeding in high-risk anorexia nervosa (BMI under 14, rapid loss, bradycardia, QTc prolongation) with continuous cardiac monitoring on a paediatric ward (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders; RANZCP Eating Disorders CPG).

options.text: Check phosphate every 48 hours and defer electrolyte checks unless the patient becomes symptomatic
options.rationale: Refeeding hypophosphataemia is a laboratory diagnosis that often precedes clinical features and can precipitate arrhythmia and respiratory failure; symptom-triggered testing is unsafe in a patient with baseline low phosphate (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

options.text: Prescribe empirical oral phosphate replacement and defer routine electrolyte monitoring for the first 72 hours
options.rationale: Empirical phosphate replacement is reasonable but does not remove the need for close monitoring; the pathway is both prophylactic replacement and 12-hourly checks (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

options.text: Check a 12 lead ECG only if the pulse falls below 40 or the potassium falls below 3.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: Continuous cardiac monitoring rather than symptom-triggered ECG is the RCH standard for the first 72 hours in a patient with baseline bradycardia and QTc 470 ms; intermittent ECG misses developing arrhythmia (Source: RCH CPG: Eating Disorders).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is a shift of phosphate, potassium, magnesium and glucose into cells triggered by the insulin surge of reintroduced carbohydrate. It typically peaks between 24 and 72 hours of refeeding and can precipitate arrhythmia, respiratory failure and cardiac failure. The RCH and MARSIPAN paediatric pathways define high-risk anorexia nervosa by BMI under 14, rapid weight loss, bradycardia under 50, QTc prolongation, or baseline low phosphate or potassium. High-risk patients require 12-hourly biochemistry for the first 72 hours, continuous cardiac monitoring, prophylactic oral phosphate replacement, and a slow calorie ladder starting around 1000 kcal per day.
key_points: Refeeding shifts peak between 24 and 72 hours
12-hourly phosphate, magnesium, potassium and glucose in high-risk
Continuous cardiac monitoring for BMI under 14 or QTc over 460 ms
Prophylactic oral phosphate and thiamine at admission
Slow calorie ladder starting around 1000 kcal per day
explanation.pearls: The RCH threshold for continuous cardiac monitoring in adolescent anorexia is a resting pulse under 50, QTc over 460 ms, or any postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic; meeting any one of these commits the patient to a HDU-level of surveillance during refeeding.

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation in acute mania in an adult inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 32 year old teacher on a mental health inpatient unit under an assessment order. He presents with 10 days of reduced sleep to 2 hours nightly, pressured speech, grandiose plans to buy a farm, hypersexual disinhibition, and expenditure of 40,000 dollars on credit cards. He has one prior similar episode 3 years ago that responded well to lithium. His current medications are none.

He drinks 1 standard drink weekly, is well hydrated, and denies current suicidal ideation. His weight is 78 kg. Baseline sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 4.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), creatinine is 72 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 90 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH is 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), calcium is 2.35 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), and BhCG (or equivalent pregnancy test surrogate for a male: not applicable).

ECG shows sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation. He is not currently on any other psychotropic medication and has never been on valproate.

data_table.Baseline biochemistry: Sodium 140, potassium 4.0, creatinine 72 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR over 90, TSH 2.1 (0.4 to 4.0), calcium 2.35 (2.15 to 2.55)
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial dose regimen for lithium?

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate 1500 mg orally as a single loading dose then daily 500 mg with a level in 24 hours
options.rationale: Lithium loading doses risk supratherapeutic levels and are not recommended; steady state is reached over 5 to 7 days and titration relies on 12-hour troughs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate 250 mg orally at night with a level drawn 24 hours after the first dose
options.rationale: A subtherapeutic starting dose delays symptom control in acute mania and a 24 hour post-dose level does not represent the 12-hour trough that guides titration; this delays effective treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate 750 mg orally at night with a level drawn at 12 hours post dose after 5 days
options.rationale: In acute mania with normal renal function the AU practice is to initiate lithium at a target-directed dose of around 750 to 1000 mg nocte titrated by a 12-hour trough drawn 5 to 7 days after each dose change, aiming for a level of 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Bipolar CPG).

options.text: Commence lithium carbonate 250 mg orally three times daily to spread the dose evenly
options.rationale: Once nightly dosing is preferred to divided dosing because it reduces peak renal exposure and long-term nephrotoxicity risk without loss of efficacy; three times daily dosing is outdated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Defer lithium and start sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily as first-line for acute mania
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is a reasonable alternative but the patient has a prior good response to lithium and preserved renal function; that history makes lithium first-line rather than a switch to valproate (Source: RANZCP Bipolar CPG).

explanation.summary: Lithium remains a first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania in adults with preserved renal function, especially when there is a documented prior good response. Australian practice is to initiate at 750 to 1000 mg nocte as a single dose and re-check the 12-hour trough level after 5 to 7 days, aiming for 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L for acute mania and 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance. Once-daily nocte dosing gives lower renal peak exposure than divided dosing and is now standard. Baseline workup includes urea electrolytes creatinine, eGFR, TSH, calcium, and ECG, all repeated at 3 to 6 monthly intervals during maintenance.
key_points: Target-directed dose 750 to 1000 mg nocte in normal renal function
12-hour trough drawn at 5 to 7 days to guide titration
Acute mania target 0.8 to 1.2 mmol/L
Once nightly dosing lowers long-term nephrotoxicity risk
Baseline TSH, calcium, eGFR, ECG before initiation
explanation.pearls: The steady-state assumption behind a 12-hour trough is only valid after 5 half-lives, which for lithium in normal renal function is 5 to 7 days; a level drawn at 48 hours will systematically underestimate the eventual steady state and drives inappropriate over-titration.

subtopic_detail: First-line management of PTSD in an adult veteran
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 41 year old woman who served in the Australian Defence Force and was discharged 4 years ago. Over the last 8 months she has had recurrent intrusive memories of an IED incident, nightmares 5 nights a week, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, avoidance of driving on freeways, and a persistent sense of foreshortened future. She does not use alcohol or illicit drugs and has never had psychotic symptoms.

She is up to date on her Open Arms sessions but has attended 4 in the last 6 months only. Her PCL-5 score is 52 and her PHQ-9 is 12 with no active suicidal ideation. She is otherwise well, on no medication, and has no history of bipolar disorder or first-degree family history of mood disorders. Sleep-onset insomnia and impaired concentration are limiting her role as a supply chain analyst.

She is willing to consider both psychological therapy and pharmacotherapy and asks what should be tried first.

data_table.Screening scores: PCL-5 52; PHQ-9 12 with no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Function: Sleep-onset insomnia and impaired concentration limiting employment

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally each morning as monotherapy for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Sertraline is second-line for PTSD when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable, refused or has failed; monotherapy pharmacotherapy first-line is not the AU standard (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for structured trauma-focused CBT delivered over 8 to 12 weekly sessions
options.rationale: AU and international guidelines place trauma-focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) as first-line treatment for PTSD ahead of pharmacotherapy because effect sizes are larger and gains are more durable (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines; RANZCP PTSD CPG).

options.text: Commence prazosin 1 mg orally each night for nightmares as monotherapy
options.rationale: Prazosin is adjunctive for PTSD nightmares but does not treat re-experiencing, avoidance, or hyperarousal broadly; it is not first-line monotherapy (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg orally at night for hyperarousal as monotherapy
options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotics as PTSD monotherapy are not supported by the AU guideline and carry metabolic and sedation risks unlikely to be justified before trauma-focused therapy has been offered (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg orally at night for sleep and startle symptom control
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in PTSD as they worsen long-term outcomes, blunt exposure-based recovery, and carry dependence risk in a veteran population with elevated substance use rates (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, with re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal persisting more than one month. The Phoenix Australia guideline places structured trauma-focused psychological therapies (TF-CBT, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) as first-line treatment ahead of pharmacotherapy in both civilian and veteran populations. Sertraline, paroxetine, and venlafaxine are second-line when trauma-focused therapy is unavailable or has failed. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated because they worsen long-term outcomes.
key_points: TF-CBT, CPT and EMDR are first-line for PTSD
Sertraline is second-line when psychological therapy fails
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are contraindicated
Prazosin has an adjunctive role for nightmares only
Screen with PCL-5 and monitor for comorbid depression
explanation.pearls: Trauma-focused psychological therapies deliver an effect size of around 1.4 for PTSD symptoms in the Phoenix Australia meta-analysis, roughly twice that of pharmacotherapy alone, which is why they lead the algorithm even in veteran cohorts where medication adherence is often better than therapy attendance.

subtopic_detail: SSRI dose escalation strategy in an adult with OCD
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 27 year old teacher with a 2 year history of contamination obsessions and hand-washing compulsions occupying more than 3 hours daily. He has been on fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning for 12 weeks with only marginal reduction in his Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale score from 26 to 22 and no functional improvement.

He attends weekly sessions with a clinical psychologist for exposure and response prevention. He has no history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no suicidal ideation. Sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), liver function tests are within normal limits, and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 410 ms. He does not use alcohol, illicit drugs, or over-the-counter serotonergic agents.

He is adherent to the current fluoxetine dose, tolerating it without adverse effects, and asks what should happen next.

data_table.Current pharmacotherapy: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning for 12 weeks
data_table.Baseline labs: Sodium 140 (135 to 145); LFTs within normal limits; ECG sinus with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Increase fluoxetine to 60 mg orally each morning and continue current ERP therapy
options.rationale: OCD often requires SSRI doses above the standard depression range, with fluoxetine up to 80 mg the AU-recommended target, and a 12 week trial at the maximum tolerated dose is required before declaring a treatment failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP OCD CPG).

options.text: Switch to sertraline 50 mg orally each morning as SSRI monotherapy for OCD
options.rationale: Switching SSRIs before a full 12 week trial at maximum tolerated dose is premature; OCD needs both higher doses and longer trials than depression before an SSRI is deemed to have failed (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

options.text: Add risperidone 1 mg orally each night to current fluoxetine 20 mg regimen
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for SSRI non-response after full-dose full-duration trial, particularly for OCD with tic-related features; augmentation before dose optimisation is not first-line (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

options.text: Discontinue fluoxetine and refer for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
options.rationale: TMS for OCD is a last-line intervention reserved for treatment-resistant disease after multiple failed SSRI trials and augmentation; discontinuing pharmacotherapy before dose optimisation is not indicated (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

options.text: Discontinue fluoxetine and commence clomipramine 25 mg orally each night instead
options.rationale: Clomipramine is effective in OCD but carries greater anticholinergic, cardiac and seizure risks than SSRIs, and is reserved for failure of two SSRIs at optimised dose and duration (Source: RANZCP OCD CPG).

explanation.summary: Obsessive-compulsive disorder responds to SSRIs at doses higher than those used for depression and requires longer trials before non-response is declared. The AU recommendation is to titrate to the maximum tolerated dose (fluoxetine up to 80 mg, sertraline up to 200 mg, escitalopram up to 40 mg with ECG surveillance) and continue for at least 12 weeks at that dose before switching or augmenting. Exposure and response prevention therapy is the psychological treatment of choice and runs in parallel with pharmacotherapy. Augmentation with a low-dose antipsychotic is reserved for confirmed SSRI failure after adequate dose and duration.
key_points: OCD SSRI doses run higher than depression doses
Fluoxetine target up to 80 mg orally daily
12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose before failure declared
ERP therapy runs in parallel with SSRI
Antipsychotic augmentation only after true SSRI failure
explanation.pearls: A common OCD pitfall is switching SSRIs at 12 weeks on a sub-therapeutic dose because clinicians extrapolate from depression trials; the trial clock only starts once the OCD-target dose is reached, so a 12 week trial at 20 mg fluoxetine is a 0 week OCD trial.

subtopic_detail: First-line stimulant selection in newly diagnosed adult ADHD
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an adult ADHD clinic reviewing a 26 year old software developer with newly diagnosed combined presentation ADHD confirmed by a structured DIVA-5 interview, collateral from her mother, and school reports demonstrating longstanding inattention from primary school onwards.

She is otherwise well, on no medication, and has a resting pulse of 76 and a blood pressure of 122/74 mmHg. She has no personal or family history of arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, structural heart disease, glaucoma, or bipolar disorder. She has no history of substance use disorder and no current comorbid psychiatric diagnosis. Her weight is 62 kg. TSH is within normal limits and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms.

She wants to try medication for the first time and asks what will be started.

data_table.Assessment: DIVA-5 confirms combined presentation ADHD; collateral from mother; primary school reports consistent
data_table.Cardiac screen: Pulse 76; BP 122/74 mmHg; no family history of sudden death or cardiomyopathy; ECG sinus with QTc 400 ms
data_table.Comorbidities: No substance use disorder, no bipolar disorder, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg orally each morning off-label for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Bupropion has modest evidence for adult ADHD and is not first-line; it is reserved for stimulant failure or when a comorbid tobacco use disorder or depression steers the choice (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally each morning and review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a second-line non-stimulant option reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or substance use disorder concerns; effect size is lower than stimulants (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning and review at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) are first-line pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD with no substance use disorder or cardiac contraindication; lisdexamfetamine 30 mg is a standard starting dose per AU authority prescribing guidance (Source: RANZCP ADHD CPG; AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence guanfacine extended release 1 mg orally at night as monotherapy
options.rationale: Guanfacine is TGA-registered for paediatric ADHD only and is not first-line for adult ADHD; it is used as an adjunct in select paediatric cases with tic disorder or oppositional features (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Defer pharmacotherapy and offer 12 weeks of cognitive behavioural therapy alone
options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone has smaller effect sizes than stimulant pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD; the AU algorithm places stimulant pharmacotherapy first with psychological therapy as an adjunct once symptom control is achieved (Source: AADPA ADHD Guideline).
source_refs: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires DSM-5 criteria that includes onset of symptoms in the developmental period, corroborated by collateral or school reports, and pervasive dysfunction across multiple settings. First-line pharmacotherapy in the AADPA Australian guideline is a long-acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) titrated over 4 to 6 weeks with cardiac and mental state monitoring. Non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine in paediatrics, clonidine) are second-line for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or when there is a concurrent substance use disorder. Contraindications to stimulants include untreated hypertension, arrhythmia, structural heart disease, glaucoma, and current stimulant misuse.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant is first-line for adult ADHD
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg or methylphenidate XR standard starts
Atomoxetine is second-line for stimulant intolerance
Cardiac screen with pulse, BP, and personal or family history before starting
Review at 4 weeks then titrate to symptom control
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring gut activation and gives a smoother release curve than dexamfetamine, which reduces afternoon rebound irritability and lowers diversion potential; this profile is why it is the AU authority-approved default first-choice stimulant in adult ADHD.

sources.label: AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: First-line management of generalised anxiety disorder in an adult
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 38 year old primary school teacher with a 14 month history of excessive worry about work performance, her children's safety, and household finances. She describes muscle tension in her shoulders, sleep-onset insomnia, difficulty concentrating on marking, and irritability that has affected her relationship with her partner.

She does not use alcohol, illicit drugs, or nicotine. Her caffeine intake is 1 flat white in the morning. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder and no psychotic symptoms. TSH is 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), ferritin is 68 microgram/L (30 to 500), full blood count is within normal limits, and 12 lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms.

Her GAD-7 score is 16 and her PHQ-9 is 8 with no suicidal ideation. Her symptoms are persistent, present most days for the last 14 months, and cause significant impairment. She has not previously tried medication or psychological therapy and asks what should happen next.

data_table.Screening scores: GAD-7 16; PHQ-9 8 with no suicidal ideation
data_table.Baseline labs: TSH 1.9 (0.4 to 4.0); ferritin 68 microgram/L (30 to 500); FBC within normal limits; ECG sinus QTc 400 ms
data_table.Substance use: 1 flat white daily; no alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment recommendation?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for symptom control ongoing
options.rationale: Regular benzodiazepine use in GAD carries dependence risk, blunts cognitive engagement in therapy, and is not first-line; short courses can bridge acute distress but not as an initial monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for structured cognitive behavioural therapy over 8 to 12 weekly sessions
options.rationale: AU and international guidelines recommend CBT as first-line for adult GAD given its effect size comparable to SSRIs and superior durability of gains after treatment ends; pharmacotherapy is added if CBT is unavailable, refused, or gives partial response (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

options.text: Commence pregabalin 75 mg orally twice daily as GAD monotherapy long-term
options.rationale: Pregabalin is second-line for GAD with dependence potential and PBS restrictions in AU; it is reserved for SSRI or SNRI failure or intolerance rather than initial monotherapy (Source: RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

options.text: Commence quetiapine 50 mg orally each night for anxiety and sleep monotherapy
options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotic monotherapy for GAD is not first-line and carries metabolic and sedation risks not justified before evidence-based first-line options are tried (Source: RANZCP Generalised Anxiety CPG).

options.text: Recommend a repeat GAD-7 score in 6 weeks without any active intervention
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is only appropriate for mild anxiety with recent onset and mild functional impact; this patient has 14 months of symptoms, a GAD-7 of 16, and significant impairment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis when excessive worry that is difficult to control persists for at least 6 months and is accompanied by at least 3 of muscle tension, restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, and sleep disturbance. AU guidelines recommend CBT as first-line for moderate GAD given comparable acute efficacy to pharmacotherapy and greater durability of gains after treatment. SSRIs (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) are first-line pharmacotherapy when CBT is unavailable, refused, or insufficient. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term bridging, and pregabalin is second-line.
key_points: CBT is first-line for moderate GAD
SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy when CBT unavailable
Benzodiazepines are short-term bridging only
Pregabalin is second-line
GAD-7 of 15 or above indicates severe anxiety
explanation.pearls: CBT gains in GAD are more durable than SSRI gains once treatment ends: 12 month post-treatment remission rates are around 60 percent for CBT versus 40 percent for SSRI-only, which is why the AU algorithm favours the psychological arm even in patients willing to take medication.

subtopic_detail: Chronic insomnia management in an older adult
stem:
You are the GP seeing a 72 year old retired librarian with an 8 month history of difficulty initiating sleep, taking around 90 minutes to fall asleep on most nights, with 3 to 4 nocturnal awakenings and total sleep time of around 4.5 hours. She feels unrefreshed on waking and fatigued through the day.

She has no history of restless legs, snoring, witnessed apnoeas, or excessive daytime sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (score 6). Her caffeine intake is one flat white at 08:00 only. She does not use alcohol. She takes rosuvastatin 20 mg orally each night and perindopril 4 mg orally each morning. TSH, ferritin, sodium, and eGFR are within normal limits. Her PHQ-9 is 5 and her GAD-7 is 4.

Her bedroom is warm, she watches television in bed until she feels drowsy, and her spouse reports she takes daytime naps of 60 to 90 minutes. She has not tried any behavioural changes or medication for the sleep problem.

data_table.Sleep pattern: Sleep onset latency 90 minutes; 3 to 4 nocturnal awakenings; total sleep time 4.5 hours
data_table.Comorbidities and medications: Rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte; perindopril 4 mg mane; TSH, ferritin, sodium, eGFR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia over 6 to 8 weekly sessions
options.rationale: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is first-line for chronic insomnia in adults of any age, has larger durable effect sizes than pharmacotherapy, and specifically avoids the fall, cognition, and dependence risks that make hypnotic use hazardous in older adults (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

options.text: Commence temazepam 10 mg orally each night for ongoing use over 12 weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics in older adults increase falls, hip fracture, and cognitive impairment; ongoing use is not first-line and violates the Beers Criteria age-related deprescribing recommendations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence zopiclone 7.5 mg orally each night for ongoing use over 12 weeks
options.rationale: Non-benzodiazepine Z-drugs carry the same falls and cognitive risks as benzodiazepines in older adults and are not first-line for chronic insomnia when CBT-I is available (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 15 mg orally each night for its sedative effect at low dose
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is not first-line for insomnia in the absence of a mood disorder; it carries weight gain, dry mouth, and daytime somnolence, and is off-label for primary insomnia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg orally at night for 13 weeks trial
options.rationale: Prolonged-release melatonin is a reasonable pharmacological option in adults over 55 with primary insomnia but is second-line to CBT-I when CBT-I is available; effect size is modest (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis when dissatisfaction with sleep quality or quantity persists at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months with daytime consequences. AU and international guidelines place CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) as first-line treatment for adults of all ages, delivered over 6 to 8 sessions covering sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and sleep hygiene. Pharmacological options are second-line and in older adults carry an especially unfavourable balance because of fall, fracture, and cognitive impairment risk. Prolonged-release melatonin has modest evidence in over-55s; benzodiazepine and Z-drug hypnotics are Beers-listed as generally avoid in older adults.
key_points: CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia at any age
Sessions cover sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive work
Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are Beers-listed avoid in older adults
Prolonged-release melatonin is second-line in over-55s
Exclude sleep apnoea, restless legs, and depression
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction paradoxically improves total sleep time by consolidating fragmented sleep: an older adult sleeping 4.5 hours across 8 hours in bed is prescribed a 5 hour time-in-bed window that shifts homeostatic sleep drive back to their favour, with the window widened only as sleep efficiency exceeds 85 percent.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine rechallenge after benign ethnic neutropenia investigation
stem:
You are the psychiatry advanced trainee reviewing a 34 year old man of West African ancestry with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has failed adequate 6 week trials of olanzapine 20 mg orally daily and risperidone 6 mg orally daily. Attempted clozapine titration 3 months ago was stopped on week 6 when the neutrophil count fell to 1.4 x10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), classified as amber in the Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service (CPMS).

After the discontinuation the neutrophil count returned to 1.6 x10^9/L and has remained between 1.3 and 1.8 x10^9/L across five samples over 12 weeks with normal white cell function on cytology. He has no history of infection, splenomegaly, or medication other than clozapine that would explain neutropenia.

Hematology has reviewed and issued a formal report of benign ethnic neutropenia (BEN), noting a Duffy-null phenotype and a stable ANC in his usual range that predated any antipsychotic exposure. He is psychiatrically deteriorating on his current regimen with escalating persecutory delusions and command auditory hallucinations, and the family have requested clozapine rechallenge.

data_table.Neutrophil trend: 1.4 x10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5) on week 6 clozapine; 1.3 to 1.8 x10^9/L across 5 samples over 12 weeks off
data_table.Hematology report: Benign ethnic neutropenia with Duffy-null phenotype; predates antipsychotic exposure
data_table.Prior antipsychotic trials: Olanzapine 20 mg 6 weeks failed; risperidone 6 mg 6 weeks failed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step for antipsychotic therapy?

options.text: Permanently list the patient as clozapine-ineligible on CPMS and continue current oral risperidone
options.rationale: Permanent ineligibility applies to a red result of true drug-induced neutropenia, not to a haematologist-confirmed BEN diagnosis; excluding rechallenge denies effective therapy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (Source: Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service Protocol).

options.text: Commence lithium 400 mg orally at night to boost the neutrophil count while continuing risperidone
options.rationale: Lithium can raise the neutrophil count but does not address the underlying treatment resistance and is not a substitute for clozapine in genuine treatment-resistant schizophrenia (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

options.text: Commence combination olanzapine 20 mg with amisulpride 400 mg orally as antipsychotic polypharmacy
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy carries higher metabolic and extrapyramidal burden without evidence of superiority to clozapine monotherapy in treatment resistance; it is not a substitute for clozapine when BEN pathway is available (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy as monotherapy for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
options.rationale: ECT is an adjunct for clozapine-augmentation in schizophrenia, not a first-choice monotherapy when clozapine has not yet had an adequate trial under an appropriate monitoring pathway (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

options.text: Register the patient on the BEN monitoring pathway of CPMS and recommence clozapine at 12.5 mg orally at night
options.rationale: Australian CPMS has a specific BEN pathway with a lower ANC threshold (1.0 x10^9/L amber, 0.5 x10^9/L red) confirmed by haematology; rechallenge is standard when prior neutropenia is attributable to BEN and treatment resistance is established (Source: Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service Protocol; RANZCP Antipsychotic CPG).

explanation.summary: Benign ethnic neutropenia is a genetically determined lower baseline neutrophil count seen in around 25 to 50 percent of people of African, Middle Eastern, and West Indian ancestry, associated with the Duffy-null (DARC) phenotype. It reflects reduced peripheral neutrophil pool with preserved marrow reserve and no increased infection risk. The Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service maintains a specific BEN pathway with lower amber (1.0 x10^9/L) and red (0.5 x10^9/L) thresholds, activated after formal haematology confirmation. Rechallenge is appropriate when a prior discontinuation was on standard thresholds but the neutropenia is attributable to BEN and treatment resistance to two adequate non-clozapine trials is established.
key_points: BEN affects 25 to 50 percent of African-ancestry individuals
Duffy-null phenotype with reduced peripheral neutrophil pool
CPMS BEN pathway: amber 1.0, red 0.5 x10^9/L
Rechallenge appropriate after haematology confirmation of BEN
Preserved marrow reserve with no increased infection risk
explanation.pearls: The Duffy-null phenotype confers relative resistance to Plasmodium vivax malaria, which is the selective pressure driving its high prevalence in West African populations; the associated neutropenia is a benign incidental phenotype, not a haematological pathology, and the CPMS BEN pathway exists so that this evolutionary quirk does not deny effective psychiatric treatment.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 42 year old woman with schizoaffective disorder brought in with 12 hours of confusion, agitation, tremor, and rigidity. Her regular medications are olanzapine 20 mg orally at night and paroxetine 40 mg orally each morning. Yesterday her GP added tramadol 50 mg orally three times daily for lower back pain following a work injury.

On arrival her pulse is 128, blood pressure is 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate is 22, SpO2 is 98 percent on room air, and temperature is 39.4 degrees Celsius. Her pupils are 6 mm and reactive. There is bilateral lower limb hypertonicity with sustained clonus, particularly at the ankles. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ in the lower limbs. She has intermittent horizontal ocular oscillations. Bowel sounds are hyperactive.

Creatine kinase is 780 unit/L (30 to 250), sodium is 141 mmol/L (135 to 145), and white cell count is 12.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0). She does not use illicit drugs and has had no missed antipsychotic doses in the last week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 168/102 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurological signs: Pupils 6 mm reactive, bilateral lower limb hypertonicity with sustained ankle clonus, DTR 4+, intermittent horizontal ocular oscillations, hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Recent medication change: Tramadol 50 mg three times daily added yesterday

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis and its most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; cease paroxetine and tramadol and give cyproheptadine 12 mg oral first dose
options.rationale: The Hunter criteria are met with tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible or sustained clonus in the setting of a serotonergic drug addition (tramadol) to an SSRI; lower-limb-dominant rigidity, mydriasis, and hyperactive bowel sounds discriminate this from NMS which has lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia and normoactive to reduced bowel sounds (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Antipsychotic Adverse Effects CPG).

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; cease olanzapine and give IV dantrolene at 2.5 mg per kg dose
options.rationale: NMS classically shows lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, higher CK (often over 1000 and rising to 10,000), and evolves over days to weeks rather than 12 hours after a serotonergic addition; the neuromuscular pattern here does not fit NMS (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Adverse Effects CPG).

options.text: Anticholinergic toxicity; cease paroxetine and give IV physostigmine 1 mg to reverse toxicity
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxicity presents with dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention, and delirium without clonus or hyperreflexia; the current picture with sustained clonus, hyperreflexia and hyperactive bowel sounds is the opposite pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia; cease olanzapine and give IV dantrolene at 2.5 mg per kg loading dose
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia requires exposure to a volatile anaesthetic agent or depolarising muscle relaxant which has not occurred; this diagnosis is not supported by the clinical context (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxicity; give IV fluids and IV diazepam titrated to sedation without change
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic toxicity requires a stimulant exposure not present here, does not classically produce sustained clonus, and does not address the causative interaction between paroxetine and tramadol (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome overlap in fever, autonomic instability, and altered mental state but are separated on neuromuscular examination. Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria met by tremor, hyperreflexia, and inducible or sustained clonus in the presence of a serotonergic agent) is lower-limb dominant, brisk-reflex, hyperactive bowel sounds, mydriasis, and typically evolves over hours after a drug addition. NMS is upper and lower body lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, hypoactive bowel sounds, and typically evolves over days to weeks after a dopamine antagonist. Tramadol is a common triggering agent when added to an SSRI or SNRI. Management is drug withdrawal, supportive care with cooling and fluids, and cyproheptadine as a serotonin 5HT2A antagonist for moderate to severe cases.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, clonus, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, hypoactive bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome evolves in hours; NMS in days to weeks
Tramadol plus SSRI is a common trigger
Cyproheptadine 12 mg oral first dose in moderate to severe cases
explanation.pearls: Sustained clonus at the ankles in the setting of a recent serotonergic drug addition is the single most specific bedside sign for serotonin syndrome in the Hunter criteria; a normally reflexed patient on an SSRI with fever after opiate addition is far more likely to have serotonin syndrome than NMS or sepsis.

subtopic_detail: Augmentation choice for treatment-resistant depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health clinic reviewing a 54 year old warehouse supervisor with major depressive disorder. His current episode is 9 months long and has failed 8 weeks of sertraline 200 mg orally daily then 10 weeks of venlafaxine 300 mg orally daily; his current PHQ-9 is 19 with anhedonia, early morning waking, and 6 kg weight loss.

He has no history of bipolar disorder or psychosis and no active suicidal ideation. He has attended 14 sessions of interpersonal therapy over the last 5 months with only partial benefit. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine is 84 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 90, TSH is 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), and ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 415 ms. Weight is 82 kg.

He drinks 2 standard drinks weekly, does not use illicit drugs, and asks about the next medication step.

data_table.Symptom severity: PHQ-9 19; 9 month episode; no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Prior trials: Sertraline 200 mg 8 weeks failed; venlafaxine 300 mg 10 weeks failed; 14 sessions IPT partial benefit
data_table.Baseline labs: Sodium 138, creatinine 84 micromol/L, eGFR over 90, TSH 2.0, QTc 415 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Refer for deep brain stimulation of the subgenual cingulate as neurosurgical option
options.rationale: Deep brain stimulation is an investigational last-line intervention for depression that has failed multiple pharmacological, psychological, and neuromodulation options including ECT; it is not appropriate as third-line therapy (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

options.text: Add fluoxetine 20 mg orally each morning to the current venlafaxine 300 mg regimen
options.rationale: SSRI plus SNRI combination has additive serotonergic risk without robust efficacy evidence; it is not a recognised augmentation strategy and increases serotonin syndrome risk (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

options.text: Switch venlafaxine to fluoxetine 40 mg orally each morning as a third SSRI trial
options.rationale: A third serotonergic monotherapy trial after adequate SSRI and SNRI trials has diminishing yield; augmentation strategies have higher response rates than a further switch in this scenario (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

options.text: Add clonazepam 0.5 mg orally each night as anxiolytic augmentation to venlafaxine
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine augmentation is not an evidence-based strategy for depression treatment resistance and carries dependence risk; it addresses insomnia not depressive core symptoms (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG).

options.text: Continue venlafaxine 300 mg and add lithium 500 mg at night with level in 5 to 7 days
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is the most evidence-supported strategy for antidepressant-resistant unipolar depression with a number needed to treat of around 4 for response, and remains AU first-line augmentation ahead of antipsychotic augmentation in the RANZCP algorithm (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorder CPG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two adequate trials of antidepressants from different classes at optimal dose and duration. AU RANZCP guidelines place lithium augmentation and second-generation antipsychotic augmentation (aripiprazole, quetiapine XR, olanzapine) at the top of the third-line pharmacotherapy algorithm, with lithium having the largest evidence base and a number needed to treat of around 4 for response. Baseline renal function, TSH, calcium, and ECG are checked before initiation and a 12 hour trough level is drawn 5 to 7 days after each dose change targeting 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for augmentation. ECT is reserved for further failure or when acute severity demands rapid response.
key_points: Treatment-resistant depression: failure of 2 adequate trials from different classes
Lithium augmentation is the most evidence-supported strategy
Target lithium level 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for augmentation
Aripiprazole, quetiapine XR are alternative augmenting agents
ECT reserved for further failure or severe presentations
explanation.pearls: The lithium augmentation trial rule is that non-response at 4 weeks of a therapeutic level (over 0.4 mmol/L) predicts non-response overall, so serial 12 hour trough measurement matters more for augmentation adherence checks than for chasing a specific target within the lower range.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain in a young patient on olanzapine
stem:
You are the early psychosis registrar reviewing a 22 year old university student with first-episode psychosis, on olanzapine 15 mg orally at night for 6 months following a good clinical response. His weight has increased from 74 kg to 92 kg over that period with a rise in fasting glucose from 4.8 to 6.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), triglycerides from 1.2 to 3.8 mmol/L (below 1.7), and waist circumference from 88 cm to 104 cm.

He remains asymptomatic from a psychiatric perspective with no positive symptoms, no negative symptoms of concern, and full functional recovery. He has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no diabetes, and no other metabolic disease. His current medications are olanzapine 15 mg only. He is engaged in a supervised exercise programme with an accredited exercise physiologist and has completed a Nutrition Australia dietary intervention over the last 3 months without weight loss.

Blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg, ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 425 ms, and he is willing to consider a medication change if it will reverse the metabolic trajectory.

data_table.Anthropometry and metabolic: Weight 74 to 92 kg over 6 months; waist 88 to 104 cm; BP 138/86 mmHg
data_table.Biochemistry trend: Fasting glucose 4.8 to 6.4 mmol/L; triglycerides 1.2 to 3.8 mmol/L (below 1.7)
data_table.Lifestyle: 3 months supervised exercise physiologist plus Nutrition Australia diet with no weight loss

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step to address the metabolic profile?

options.text: Continue olanzapine 15 mg and add metformin 500 mg orally twice daily as adjunct
options.rationale: Metformin adjunct has modest weight-attenuating effect (2 to 3 kg over 3 months) but does not match the effect of an olanzapine to aripiprazole switch and does not address the underlying receptor pharmacology driving the weight gain (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.text: Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole 15 mg orally each morning with 4 week cross-titration
options.rationale: Switching to a metabolically favourable antipsychotic (aripiprazole, ziprasidone or lurasidone) is the most effective single intervention for antipsychotic-induced weight gain when lifestyle measures have failed and psychiatric stability allows switching; the RANZCP EPPIC algorithm places switching ahead of pharmacological adjuncts (Source: RANZCP Psychosis CPG; Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.text: Reduce olanzapine to 10 mg orally at night and continue the current lifestyle programme
options.rationale: Dose reduction of olanzapine has weak dose-response for weight gain and risks psychiatric relapse in a stable first-episode patient; a switch to a metabolically favourable agent is more effective (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.text: Continue olanzapine 15 mg and refer for bariatric surgery preoperative workup pathway
options.rationale: Bariatric surgery is not indicated for a BMI in the mid-30s where a reversible pharmacological cause is present and untried; addressing the pharmacological driver is the correct sequence (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.text: Continue olanzapine 15 mg and add orlistat 120 mg orally three times daily with meals
options.rationale: Orlistat has a small weight effect and gastrointestinal adverse profile that further undermines adherence; it does not match the effect of a switch to a metabolically favourable agent (Source: Orygen Early Psychosis Guidelines).
source_refs: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain and metabolic syndrome are common with olanzapine and clozapine because of histamine H1 and 5HT2C antagonism driving appetite and adiposity. When lifestyle measures fail and the psychiatric picture is stable, the most effective single intervention is switching to a metabolically favourable agent such as aripiprazole, ziprasidone, or lurasidone. Cross-titration over 4 weeks preserves psychiatric stability. Metformin adjunct produces modest weight attenuation but is less effective than switching. Bariatric surgery and orlistat are reserved for the setting where switching is not clinically feasible.
key_points: Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden after clozapine
Switching to aripiprazole is the most effective single intervention
Cross-titration over 4 weeks preserves psychiatric stability
Metformin adjunct produces 2 to 3 kg weight attenuation
Screen fasting glucose, lipids, waist quarterly on olanzapine
explanation.pearls: The olanzapine to aripiprazole switch typically produces 5 to 8 kg of weight loss and reversal of insulin resistance markers over 6 months, an effect size several times greater than metformin augmentation, which is why AU early psychosis programmes favour it once metabolic drift is established despite lifestyle intervention.

sources.label: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

subtopic_detail: Rate control choice in new-onset atrial fibrillation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old plumber in the acute medical assessment unit with a first presentation of atrial fibrillation. Symptom onset was 6 hours ago after his usual walk with the dog, with palpitations and mild exertional dyspnoea. He denies chest pain, syncope, or presyncope.

His pulse is irregular at 138, blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate is 18, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius. Chest auscultation is clear, JVP is not elevated, and there is no peripheral oedema. Weight is 88 kg. He has a background of hypertension controlled on perindopril 8 mg orally each morning and no known ischaemic heart disease. Ejection fraction on an echocardiogram 6 months ago for a hypertension work-up was 60 percent.

ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 138 and no ST changes or Q waves. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), TSH is 1.6 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), and troponin is undetectable on a high-sensitivity assay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse irregular at 138, BP 148/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.ECG: Atrial fibrillation at 138; no ST changes or Q waves
data_table.Baseline investigations: Sodium 138, potassium 4.4, TSH 1.6, troponin undetectable; echo 6 months ago EF 60%

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial rate-control agent?

options.text: Give oral digoxin 500 microgram loading dose then 250 microgram orally once daily
options.rationale: Digoxin is second-line to beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in AF rate control because it is ineffective at rate control on exertion and only reasonable in sedentary older patients or as add-on therapy (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

options.text: Give oral metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily titrated to resting rate under 100
options.rationale: In symptomatic AF without haemodynamic compromise and with preserved LV function, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is first-line rate control; oral loading is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable patient (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Give oral amiodarone 200 mg three times daily for one week then 200 mg once daily
options.rationale: Amiodarone is a rhythm-control not a rate-control agent and is reserved for structural heart disease when other rhythm-control options are unsuitable; it is not first-line for uncomplicated new-onset AF (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

options.text: Give IV synchronised DC cardioversion at 150 J following adequate procedural sedation
options.rationale: Emergency cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamic instability, active ischaemia, or heart failure; this patient is stable so rate control and anticoagulation decision precede any rhythm strategy (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

options.text: Give IV verapamil 5 mg slow push over 2 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: IV verapamil is a reasonable alternative rate-control choice in AF but oral therapy is preferred in a haemodynamically stable ambulant patient and IV verapamil carries risk of hypotension and bradycardia particularly if the patient later needs a beta blocker (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

explanation.summary: New-onset atrial fibrillation without haemodynamic compromise is managed with rate control, decision on anticoagulation using CHA2DS2-VA (the Australian score omitting the sex modifier), and consideration of rhythm control based on symptoms and duration. Beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are first-line rate-control agents in patients with preserved LV function. Digoxin is reserved for sedentary older patients or as add-on because it does not control the rate on exertion. Amiodarone is a rhythm-control agent for structural heart disease. Emergency electrical cardioversion is reserved for instability, ischaemia, or heart failure.
key_points: Beta blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB is first-line rate control
Digoxin is second-line and does not control exertional rate
Amiodarone is a rhythm-control agent, not rate-control
Cardioversion reserved for instability, ischaemia, heart failure
CHA2DS2-VA drives anticoagulation decision
explanation.pearls: The Australian CHA2DS2-VA score removes the female sex modifier used in the international CHA2DS2-VASc because sex-based risk elevation in AF appears to be a marker rather than an independent driver; a score of 2 or more on this AU-modified score is the threshold for anticoagulation regardless of biological sex.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic decision in an infective COPD exacerbation using Anthonisen criteria
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67 year old ex-smoker with GOLD stage 3 chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. His usual FEV1 is 42 percent predicted and he is on tiotropium 18 microgram inhaled once daily and salmeterol/fluticasone 25/250 microgram inhaled twice daily. He presents with 4 days of increased breathlessness above baseline, increased sputum volume, and a change of sputum colour from clear to yellow-green.

His pulse is 96, blood pressure is 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate is 24, SpO2 is 90 percent on room air (his baseline is 93 percent), and temperature is 37.4 degrees Celsius. Chest auscultation reveals bilateral polyphonic wheeze and mild crackles at the right base. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation and no consolidation. Arterial blood gas on room air is pH 7.36, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, and bicarbonate 26 mmol/L.

Sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145), CRP is 46 mg/L (below 5), white cell count is 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), and eosinophils are 0.16 x10^9/L. He has commenced back-up prednisolone 50 mg orally once daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/74 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 90% on room air (baseline 93%), temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Symptom triad: Increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, sputum colour change clear to yellow-green
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.36, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation without consolidation; CRP 46 mg/L (below 5); WCC 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate additional therapy?

options.text: Add ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily for 5 days
options.rationale: IV third-generation cephalosporin is reserved for severe exacerbation with hospital-level care or pneumonia, and this patient has an oral-treatable non-severe exacerbation with no consolidation on chest radiograph (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
options.rationale: Doxycycline is an appropriate alternative to amoxicillin in penicillin allergy but 14 days is longer than the 5 day eTG duration and this patient has no penicillin allergy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days
options.rationale: All three Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, sputum purulence) are met, which selects patients who benefit from antibiotics in a COPD exacerbation; amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days is first-line in eTG for non-severe infective exacerbation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; TSANZ/Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X).

options.text: Add azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for 3 days
options.rationale: Short-course azithromycin has activity against atypicals but is not first-line for infective COPD exacerbation in AU eTG; macrolide resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae is a concern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and rely on the prednisolone alone
options.rationale: All three Anthonisen criteria present define the subgroup of COPD exacerbation that derives clear antibiotic benefit; withholding antibiotics forgoes an evidence-based recovery gain (Source: TSANZ COPD-X).

explanation.summary: Antibiotic decisions in COPD exacerbation use the Anthonisen criteria of increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and sputum purulence. Patients with all three (type 1) or with sputum purulence plus one other (type 2) benefit from antibiotics; type 3 patients with only one criterion do not clearly benefit. First-line oral therapy in AU eTG for a non-severe infective exacerbation is amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days, or doxycycline in penicillin allergy. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally daily for 5 days) shorten exacerbation duration and reduce relapse. IV antibiotics are reserved for severe exacerbation or pneumonia.
key_points: Anthonisen criteria: dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence
All three or two-with-purulence: benefit from antibiotics
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 5 days is first-line oral in AU
Prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days shortens exacerbation
IV antibiotics reserved for severe exacerbation or pneumonia
explanation.pearls: Sputum purulence is the single strongest predictor of bacterial infection in a COPD exacerbation and is a better trigger for antibiotics than CRP or white cell count; a clear-sputum exacerbation with a raised CRP is more likely viral or eosinophilic than bacterial and typically responds to steroid alone.

subtopic_detail: Fluid choice in adult DKA in the first hour
stem:
You are the ED registrar treating a 24 year old woman with known type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting after 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. She admits missing basal insulin for the last 3 days after her insulin pen ran out. Weight is 62 kg.

Her pulse is 122, blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate is 28 with deep Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 is 99 percent on room air, and temperature is 37.1 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. Point-of-care glucose is 26 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.7), ketones are 5.8 mmol/L, and venous blood gas shows pH 7.12 with a bicarbonate of 8 mmol/L. Sodium is 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 5.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and creatinine is 118 micromol/L (60 to 110).

ECG shows sinus tachycardia without peaked T waves. She has 2 wide-bore IV cannulae and appropriate monitoring in place. The consultant asks you to prescribe the immediate resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 28 with Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Biochemistry: Point-of-care glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12, HCO3 8 mmol/L, sodium 128, potassium 5.1, creatinine 118 micromol/L
data_table.Weight and access: Weight 62 kg; two wide-bore IV cannulae in situ

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate fluid to give in the first hour?

options.text: 5 percent dextrose 1000 mL IV over 60 minutes as the initial resuscitation fluid
options.rationale: Dextrose-containing fluids are reserved for when the plasma glucose falls below 14 mmol/L during the insulin infusion; giving dextrose as first-hour resuscitation is inappropriate at a glucose of 26 mmol/L (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1000 mL IV over 60 minutes as the first resuscitation bolus
options.rationale: AU adult DKA pathways recommend 0.9 percent sodium chloride as the initial resuscitation fluid at approximately 1000 mL over the first hour to restore intravascular volume and initiate osmotic correction; potassium is added to subsequent bags once serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Compound sodium lactate (Hartmann's) 1000 mL IV over 60 minutes as the initial resuscitation fluid
options.rationale: Hartmann's solution contains lactate that will be metabolised to bicarbonate and may transiently worsen glycaemic and osmolar shifts; AU pathways specify 0.9 percent sodium chloride first before considering balanced solutions (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

options.text: 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 100 mL IV over 30 minutes for acidosis correction
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate in DKA is reserved for pH under 6.9 and is not recommended for pH 7.12; it worsens intracellular acidosis and cerebral oedema risk (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

options.text: Insulin actrapid 6 unit IV bolus without any resuscitation fluid in the first hour
options.rationale: Fixed-rate insulin infusion (0.1 unit/kg/hour) not bolus is the AU recommendation, and IV fluid must be running before insulin because insulin drives potassium into cells and precipitates hypotension in the volume deplete patient (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management runs on three parallel tracks: rapid fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent sodium chloride to restore intravascular volume, fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour to reverse ketogenesis, and potassium replacement once serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L. The first-hour fluid is around 1000 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride, then a maintenance rate of 250 to 500 mL per hour with added potassium. Dextrose is introduced once plasma glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9. Insulin infusion should follow rather than precede fluid resuscitation to avoid precipitating potassium shifts in a volume deplete patient.
key_points: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1000 mL over first hour
Fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hour follows the fluid
Potassium added once serum potassium under 5.5 mmol/L
Dextrose added once plasma glucose under 14 mmol/L
Bicarbonate reserved for pH under 6.9
explanation.pearls: The AU shift from divided fluid boluses to a fixed first-hour 1000 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride reflects the finding that under-resuscitation early in DKA drives acute kidney injury and prolongs ICU stay more than the previously feared over-resuscitation drives cerebral oedema in adults, though the paediatric caution against rapid volume correction still applies.

subtopic_detail: Severity assessment in community-acquired pneumonia using CORB
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 74 year old woman in the ED brought in by ambulance after 3 days of productive cough and fever. She has a background of hypertension and osteoarthritis and lives independently at home.

On arrival she is alert but disorientated to time, her pulse is 108, blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate is 32, SpO2 is 90 percent on room air, and temperature is 38.9 degrees Celsius. Chest examination reveals bronchial breathing and coarse crackles at the right lower zone. Chest radiograph confirms right lower lobe consolidation with a small ipsilateral pleural effusion. Weight is 62 kg.

Sodium is 132 mmol/L (135 to 145), urea is 12.4 mmol/L (2.5 to 8.0), creatinine is 118 micromol/L (60 to 110), white cell count is 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), and lactate is 3.2 mmol/L (below 2.0).
