She has no known drug allergies. She has not travelled overseas and has no aspiration risk factor. She has had all age-eligible vaccinations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Biochemistry and CXR: Sodium 132, urea 12.4, creatinine 118, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), lactate 3.2 mmol/L (below 2.0); right lower lobe consolidation with small ipsilateral pleural effusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Meropenem 1 g IV eight-hourly as monotherapy for 5 days without a macrolide added to regimen
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for severe CAP with risk factors for multi-drug-resistant gram-negatives (bronchiectasis, structural lung disease, recent hospitalisation with broad-spectrum antibiotics); it is not first-line here and drives resistance pressure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate for severe CAP; the CORB score is 3 (confusion, RR over 30, systolic BP under 90) and lactate is 3.2, mandating IV therapy in an inpatient setting (Source: TSANZ CAP Guideline).

options.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as monotherapy for 5 days without a macrolide added to the regimen
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy misses atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Legionella) that account for around 15 percent of severe CAP; macrolide addition is required for severe presentations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six-hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily plus single-dose IV gentamicin
options.rationale: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (CORB score 3) requires empirical cover for Streptococcus pneumoniae, atypicals and gram-negatives; the AU eTG severe CAP regimen is benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin plus a single-dose gentamicin (or ceftriaxone plus azithromycin as an alternative) (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; TSANZ CAP Guideline).

options.text: Vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV loading dose plus flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly for staphylococcal cover
options.rationale: MRSA and staphylococcal cover is not first-line for CAP unless there is post-influenza necrotising pneumonia or bacteraemia risk factors; this misses the typical Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical spectrum (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia severity in Australia is scored with CORB (Confusion, respiratory Rate over 30, systolic Blood pressure under 90, SpO2 under 90). A score of 2 or more identifies severe CAP requiring IV therapy and inpatient care. First-line empirical therapy for severe CAP in AU eTG is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six-hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily plus single-dose gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg IV, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin as an alternative. Broader cover with meropenem or vancomycin is reserved for specific risk factors. Blood cultures and urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens are collected before antibiotic administration.
key_points: CORB scores confusion, RR over 30, systolic BP under 90, SpO2 under 90
Score 2 or more defines severe CAP
Severe CAP: benzylpenicillin + azithromycin + single-dose gentamicin
Ceftriaxone + azithromycin is the AU alternative
Blood and urinary antigens before first antibiotic dose
explanation.pearls: CORB replaced CURB-65 in AU practice because urea is not needed as an independent severity marker once respiratory rate, blood pressure and confusion have been captured; the omission avoids the delay of waiting for biochemistry before starting IV antibiotics in the septic patient.

subtopic_detail: IV iron indication in iron deficiency anaemia
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 48 year old woman with newly diagnosed iron deficiency anaemia detected on preoperative bloods for elective knee arthroplasty scheduled in 4 weeks. She has heavy menstrual bleeding managed with the levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted 12 months ago and has no gastrointestinal symptoms.

Her haemoglobin is 92 g/L (115 to 165), MCV is 74 fL (80 to 100), ferritin is 8 microgram/L (30 to 500), transferrin saturation is 6 percent (20 to 45), and CRP is 3 mg/L (below 5). Renal function, liver function, coeliac serology and faecal immunochemical test are within normal limits. She has no history of atopic dermatitis or asthma.

She has previously trialled oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg orally each morning for 8 weeks with poor gastrointestinal tolerance (nausea and abdominal cramping) and stopped after 3 weeks. She has now trialled ferrous sulfate 325 mg orally on alternate days for a further 4 weeks with better tolerance but repeat haemoglobin today has risen only from 88 to 92 g/L. She weighs 68 kg.

data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115 to 165); MCV 74 fL (80 to 100)
data_table.Iron studies: Ferritin 8 microgram/L (30 to 500); transferrin saturation 6% (20 to 45); CRP 3 mg/L (below 5)
data_table.Oral iron trial: 8 weeks ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily stopped for GI intolerance; alternate-day dosing 4 weeks with Hb rise 88 to 92 g/L only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in iron replacement?

options.text: Defer intervention and repeat full blood count after the surgery in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Preoperative iron deficiency is a modifiable risk factor for postoperative complications and higher transfusion rates; deferring intervention forgoes the AU Patient Blood Management preoperative optimisation pathway (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines Module 2).

options.text: Increase oral ferrous sulfate to 325 mg orally three times daily for a further 12 weeks
options.rationale: Higher-frequency dosing worsens tolerance without proportional gain because hepcidin blocks absorption for 24 to 48 hours after each dose; alternate-day dosing improves fractional absorption but here the timeline before surgery does not allow it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

options.text: Transfuse 2 units of red blood cells to correct the haemoglobin before surgery
options.rationale: Preoperative transfusion for a stable Hb over 80 g/L does not correct iron stores, exposes the patient to transfusion risk, and misses the correctable cause; IV iron is the AU Patient Blood Management first-line option (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines Module 2).

options.text: Administer ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose in an appropriate infusion setting
options.rationale: IV iron is indicated for iron deficiency anaemia when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when rapid replacement is required (such as before surgery in 4 weeks), or in ongoing losses that exceed oral absorption; ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg is a single-visit AU standard dose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; PBAC/NBA Iron Product Guidance).

options.text: Refer for endoscopic evaluation for occult gastrointestinal blood loss before any further treatment
options.rationale: Endoscopy is warranted in an unexplained iron deficient patient but the clear obstetric-menstrual cause with a normal faecal immunochemical test in a low-risk age group does not mandate endoscopy before treating; treatment and evaluation can proceed in parallel (Source: RACGP Iron Deficiency in Adults Guideline).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in Australia is managed first by identifying and treating the source of loss, then by replacing iron. Oral iron in a single daily or alternate-day dose is first-line for stable outpatients. IV iron is indicated when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when rapid replacement is required (surgery, third-trimester pregnancy, functional class 3 heart failure), when ongoing losses exceed oral absorption capacity, or in inflammatory bowel disease with malabsorption. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose or iron polymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single or divided dose are the standard AU parenteral options.
key_points: Investigate the cause of iron deficiency before or in parallel with treatment
IV iron for oral failure, intolerance, or rapid replacement needs
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV single dose is AU standard
Alternate-day oral dosing improves fractional absorption
Preoperative IV iron reduces postoperative transfusion
explanation.pearls: Hepcidin rises for 24 to 48 hours after an oral iron dose, which is why alternate-day dosing gives fractional absorption almost double that of daily dosing at half the gastrointestinal side effect burden; this is now the RACGP-preferred oral schedule when the clinical timeline allows.

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive choice in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 58 year old carpenter with type 2 diabetes mellitus of 8 years standing, on metformin 1 g orally twice daily. His HbA1c is 7.1 percent (below 7.0), his lipids are within target on rosuvastatin 20 mg orally each night, and his weight is 92 kg. He does not smoke and drinks 4 standard drinks a week.

Today's blood pressure over three separate visits in the last month is averaging 152/94 mmHg. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) sent last week is 12 mg/mmol (below 2.5), confirmed on a repeat first-morning sample. Serum creatinine is 88 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 90 mL/min/1.73m2, potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and sodium is 140 mmol/L (135 to 145).

He is not on any antihypertensive currently, has no known ischaemic heart disease, has no history of angioedema, and is willing to start a new medication. Retinal examination six months ago showed background diabetic retinopathy.

data_table.Ambulatory blood pressure: Average 152/94 mmHg over three visits in the last month
data_table.Renal and metabolic: eGFR over 90, creatinine 88 micromol/L, potassium 4.2, sodium 140, HbA1c 7.1% (below 7.0)
data_table.Albuminuria: uACR 12 mg/mmol (below 2.5) confirmed on repeat first-morning sample

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antihypertensive?

options.text: Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics are first-line for older non-diabetic hypertensives but do not have the renoprotective effect of an ACE inhibitor and can worsen glycaemic control at higher doses; they are second-line here (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

options.text: Amlodipine 5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers control blood pressure well but do not have the specific renoprotective effect of ACE inhibitors or ARBs in albuminuric diabetic kidney disease; they are second-line when an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

options.text: Perindopril 4 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure and potassium
options.rationale: In hypertensive type 2 diabetes with albuminuria, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) is first-line because it slows albuminuria progression and progression to end-stage kidney disease independent of blood pressure lowering; perindopril 4 mg titrated is the AU eTG regimen (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline; KDIGO Diabetes and CKD Guideline).

options.text: Bisoprolol 2.5 mg orally each morning titrated to blood pressure control
options.rationale: Beta blockers are reserved for hypertension with a specific indication (ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, AF rate control); they are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension and do not have the renoprotective specificity of an ACE inhibitor (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg orally each morning as initial monotherapy
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are fourth-line for resistant hypertension in the NHFA algorithm; they are not initial monotherapy and carry hyperkalaemia risk when combined with the ACE inhibitor typically required in albuminuric diabetes (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

explanation.summary: Hypertension in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria is managed with an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) as first-line therapy because these agents slow albuminuria and progression to end-stage kidney disease independent of blood pressure lowering. Target blood pressure in this population is under 140/90 mmHg in general and under 130/80 mmHg where tolerated (albuminuria present). Combination therapy is usually needed to reach target, adding a calcium channel blocker and/or thiazide next. SGLT2 inhibitors have additional cardiorenal benefit in diabetic kidney disease and are added when eGFR and glycaemic control allow. Beta blockers are reserved for specific indications.
key_points: ACE inhibitor is first-line in albuminuric diabetic hypertension
Target BP under 130/80 mmHg in albuminuria where tolerated
Check creatinine and potassium at 1 to 2 weeks after starting
Add CCB or thiazide next to reach target
SGLT2 inhibitor adds cardiorenal benefit in diabetic kidney disease
explanation.pearls: A rise in creatinine of up to 30 percent from baseline after starting an ACE inhibitor in albuminuric CKD is expected and is not a reason to stop; only a rise beyond 30 percent, a fall in eGFR, or a potassium above 5.5 mmol/L should trigger dose reduction or cessation.

subtopic_detail: Escalation criteria in cellulitis of the lower limb
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 54 year old warehouse worker sent from the community wound clinic with 3 days of a spreading erythema on the right shin. He describes fatigue, one episode of shaking chill overnight, and increasing calf pain despite 24 hours of cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily commenced by his GP for a small skin abrasion sustained at work.

His pulse is 108, blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate is 20, SpO2 is 97 percent on room air, and temperature is 38.2 degrees Celsius. The lower limb shows a warm confluent erythema extending from the ankle to the mid-calf with a 4 by 6 cm central area of induration and no fluctuance, blistering, or crepitus. Distal pulses are present with normal capillary refill.

His background includes type 2 diabetes on metformin with an HbA1c of 6.9 percent (below 7.0) and a chronic tinea pedis that he has not treated. He weighs 84 kg. His white cell count is 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), CRP is 148 mg/L (below 5), and creatinine is 84 micromol/L (60 to 110). He has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Local examination: Warm confluent erythema ankle to mid-calf; 4 by 6 cm area of induration; no fluctuance, blistering, or crepitus; distal pulses present
data_table.Biochemistry: WCC 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); CRP 148 mg/L (below 5); creatinine 84 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Discharge on oral clindamycin 450 mg six-hourly for 10 days with community follow-up review
options.rationale: Oral clindamycin monotherapy is not first-line for cellulitis with systemic features; C. difficile risk is high and oral therapy at home is unsafe in a septic patient failing initial oral cover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Continue oral cephalexin 500 mg six-hourly and add oral metronidazole 400 mg eight-hourly
options.rationale: Adding anaerobic cover is not indicated for uncomplicated cellulitis and continuing oral therapy that has failed at 24 hours delays effective treatment in a systemically unwell patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for IV flucloxacillin 2 g six-hourly and reassess response after 48 hours of therapy
options.rationale: Cellulitis with systemic features (fever, tachycardia, rigor) and failure of first-line oral therapy meets AU eTG criteria for IV escalation; flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly covers Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus with a switch to oral once systemically improved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Hospital in the Home Society Australia).
source_refs: Hospital in the Home Society Australia

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical debridement without further imaging or additional antibiotic cover
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis features (rapidly spreading pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, systemic toxicity requiring vasopressors) are not present; there is no indication for immediate debridement over an antibiotic escalation trial (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose plus IV meropenem 1 g eight-hourly cover
options.rationale: Empirical MRSA and broad-spectrum gram-negative cover is not indicated for community-acquired cellulitis without MRSA risk factors (recent hospitalisation, aged care residence, prior MRSA colonisation, injection drug use) (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is managed by severity: uncomplicated cellulitis without systemic features responds to oral therapy (cephalexin or dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily). Escalation to IV therapy is indicated for systemic features (fever, tachycardia, rigor, hypotension), failure of oral therapy at 24 to 48 hours, immunocompromise, or extensive involvement, with flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly the first-line agent. MRSA cover (vancomycin) is added when specific risk factors are present. Necrotising infection requires urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics, with treatment of chronic tinea pedis to reduce cellulitis recurrence. Blood cultures should be collected when systemic features are present before antibiotic administration.
key_points: Systemic features or oral failure trigger IV escalation
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly is first-line
MRSA cover added only for specific risk factors
Necrotising features mandate surgical review
Treat tinea pedis to reduce recurrence
explanation.pearls: Pain out of proportion to visible signs, crepitus, bullae, or rapidly advancing margin over hours are the necrotising fasciitis red flags that override the antibiotic-only pathway and mandate immediate surgical review; the absence of these signs in a systemically unwell patient with typical erythema selects an antibiotic escalation trial before considering theatre.

subtopic_detail: Antithrombotic choice within 24 hours of a high-risk TIA
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the ED seeing a 71 year old woman with 45 minutes of right-sided facial droop, right arm and hand weakness, and dysarthria that completely resolved before arrival 3 hours ago. She has a background of hypertension on perindopril 8 mg orally each morning, hypercholesterolaemia on rosuvastatin 20 mg orally each night, and no known ischaemic heart disease.

On examination she has a fully symmetrical face, normal power in all four limbs, no dysarthria, and no ataxia. NIH Stroke Scale is 0. Her ABCD2 score is 5 (age 60 or over 1, BP 158/90 mmHg 1, unilateral weakness 2, symptom duration 10 to 59 min 1, no diabetes 0). Her pulse is 78 in sinus rhythm on a 24 hour Holter monitor started in the ED, and echocardiogram from 12 months ago showed no left atrial enlargement or intracardiac thrombus.

CT brain shows no acute infarct or haemorrhage. CT angiogram of the head and neck shows 30 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine is 78 micromol/L (60 to 110), and platelets are 232 x10^9/L (150 to 400). She takes no antiplatelet or anticoagulant currently and has no history of gastrointestinal bleeding.

data_table.Neurological examination: NIHSS 0; full resolution of symptoms 3 hours ago; ABCD2 score 5
data_table.Imaging: CT brain no acute infarct or haemorrhage; CTA head and neck 30% left ICA stenosis
data_table.Cardiac and biochemistry: Sinus rhythm on 24 hour Holter; no LAE or thrombus on echo 12 months ago; creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110); platelets 232 x10^9/L (150 to 400)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antithrombotic regimen?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily as empirical anticoagulation for possible occult paroxysmal AF
options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation for possible occult AF is not indicated; extended rhythm monitoring is the AU standard while single antiplatelet or dual antiplatelet cover runs based on the current sinus rhythm findings (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily as monotherapy long-term without an initial loading dose given
options.rationale: Single antiplatelet monotherapy in high-risk TIA misses the early window (first 21 days) where dual antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrence; a loading dose is standard for the first day (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

options.text: Warfarin loaded at 5 mg orally daily and continued long-term targeting INR range 2 to 3
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is reserved for a cardioembolic source (AF, mechanical valve, LV thrombus); this patient is in sinus rhythm with no cardiac source, so antiplatelet not anticoagulation is indicated (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg oral load then aspirin 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg oral daily for 21 days
options.rationale: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor ischaemic stroke without indication for anticoagulation is managed with 21 days of dual antiplatelet therapy started within 24 hours of symptom onset, then long-term single antiplatelet; this reduces recurrent stroke risk based on CHANCE and POINT trial evidence adopted by the Stroke Foundation (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg plus dipyridamole 200 mg modified-release orally twice daily as long-term therapy
options.rationale: Aspirin plus dipyridamole is a reasonable long-term single-agent alternative combination but is not the AU first-line for the first 21 days after high-risk TIA; that role is filled by aspirin plus clopidogrel (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor ischaemic stroke (NIHSS under 4) without indication for anticoagulation is managed with dual antiplatelet therapy for the first 21 days followed by single antiplatelet long-term. Aspirin is loaded 300 mg then continued at 100 mg daily and clopidogrel is added at 75 mg daily (with a 300 mg loading dose in some pathways) for the 21 day window. This regimen reduces recurrent stroke over the first 90 days without a significant increase in major bleeding. Anticoagulation is reserved for cardioembolic sources (AF, mechanical valve, LV thrombus). Extended rhythm monitoring for occult paroxysmal AF is recommended in cryptogenic events.
key_points: High-risk TIA: ABCD2 score 4 or more
Dual antiplatelet for 21 days then single antiplatelet long-term
Aspirin load 300 mg then 100 mg; add clopidogrel 75 mg
Anticoagulation reserved for cardioembolic source
Extended rhythm monitoring for occult AF
explanation.pearls: The 21 day dual antiplatelet window is derived from CHANCE and POINT which showed the recurrent stroke reduction is driven by events in the first 21 days and the bleeding excess accumulates beyond it, which is why the AU pathway stops one agent at day 21 rather than day 90 as originally trialled.

subtopic_detail: Statin-associated muscle symptoms with normal creatine kinase
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 66 year old retired teacher on rosuvastatin 40 mg orally each night for secondary prevention 8 months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. She reports 6 weeks of bilateral proximal thigh aching that developed after a landscaping weekend at her daughter's house and has persisted despite modifying activity.

Power is symmetrical and preserved at 5 out of 5 on the MRC scale in all four limbs. She can rise from a chair without hand assistance and squat and rise without difficulty. Ankle jerks are present and symmetrical. Creatine kinase is 138 unit/L (30 to 250), TSH is 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 62 nmol/L (50 to 200), electrolytes are within normal limits, and eGFR is over 90.

Her LDL cholesterol on the current dose is 1.5 mmol/L (target below 1.8 for secondary prevention). She takes no other new medication, is not on grapefruit juice, has no personal or family history of muscle disease, and rates the muscle symptoms as a 3 out of 10 severity that is making her worry about being able to garden. She asks what should happen next.

data_table.Muscle examination: Bilateral proximal thigh aching; power 5/5 symmetrical; chair rise and squat without difficulty; symmetrical ankle jerks
data_table.Biochemistry: CK 138 unit/L (30 to 250); TSH 2.0 (0.4 to 4.0); vitamin D 62 nmol/L (50 to 200); eGFR over 90

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Refer for muscle biopsy to exclude an immune-mediated necrotising myopathy from current symptoms
options.rationale: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy classically presents with proximal weakness, CK over 1000, and a positive anti-HMGCR antibody; a CK of 138 with preserved power does not meet the pretest probability threshold for biopsy (Source: RCPA Autoantibody Guideline).

options.text: Continue rosuvastatin 40 mg and add coenzyme Q10 200 mg orally daily over the next 12 weeks
options.rationale: Coenzyme Q10 has been repeatedly negative in randomised trials for statin-associated muscle symptoms and is not recommended by AU or international lipid guidelines; it does not address the diagnostic uncertainty (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

options.text: Stop rosuvastatin permanently and rely on lifestyle modification alone for LDL cholesterol control
options.rationale: Secondary prevention statin therapy carries a large mortality benefit and abandonment before a rechallenge trial forgoes that benefit; the diagnostic uncertainty here does not justify permanent cessation (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

options.text: Immediately switch rosuvastatin to ezetimibe 10 mg orally daily as statin monotherapy replacement
options.rationale: Ezetimibe monotherapy delivers around 20 percent LDL reduction versus 50 percent from high-intensity statin; switching before establishing a causal link risks losing statin benefit that most patients would tolerate on rechallenge (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

options.text: Stop rosuvastatin for 4 weeks then if symptoms resolve rechallenge with rosuvastatin 5 mg nocte
options.rationale: Statin-associated muscle symptoms with normal CK are managed by a supervised statin pause of 2 to 4 weeks to establish causal linkage and then a rechallenge with a lower dose or a different statin (usually rosuvastatin at low dose given its potency), because up to 70 percent of patients with self-reported statin muscle symptoms tolerate rechallenge; secondary-prevention statin therapy must not be abandoned without a rechallenge trial (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are common (10 to 15 percent of patients on high-intensity statin) but immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is rare (around 2 to 3 per 100,000). CK measurement discriminates: a normal CK with preserved power steers toward a benign statin-associated pattern with a high pretest probability of rechallenge tolerance, while a CK over 1000 with weakness triggers workup for immune-mediated necrotising myopathy including anti-HMGCR antibody. Management of the benign pattern is a 2 to 4 week statin pause, symptom reassessment, then rechallenge at a lower dose or a different statin. Coenzyme Q10 is not effective. Ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor add-on is reserved for confirmed statin intolerance after multiple rechallenge attempts.
key_points: Normal CK with preserved power favours benign statin-associated muscle symptoms
2 to 4 week supervised pause then rechallenge at lower dose
Up to 70 percent tolerate rechallenge
Coenzyme Q10 is not effective
Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is a rare mimic
explanation.pearls: The nocebo component of statin-associated muscle symptoms is substantial: in the SAMSON and StatinWISE double-blind crossover trials, over 90 percent of the symptom burden reported on active statin was reproduced by placebo, which is why a supervised pause and blinded rechallenge remains the diagnostic strategy of choice.

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice in suspected antiphospholipid syndrome
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38 year old graphic designer with an unprovoked right lower limb proximal deep vein thrombosis confirmed on ultrasound 2 weeks ago. She was commenced on apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily in ED at the time of diagnosis.

Her past history includes two second trimester foetal losses at 22 and 24 weeks gestation, one previous transient ischaemic attack at age 32, and a livedo reticularis pattern on the outer thighs. She takes no regular medication other than the apixaban and has never smoked. She weighs 68 kg.

Urgent screening bloods sent at diagnosis have returned today. Lupus anticoagulant is positive on the diluted Russell viper venom time and confirmed on the mixing test. Anti-cardiolipin IgG is 68 GPL (below 40) and anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I IgG is 92 units (below 20). Full blood count, renal function, and liver function are within normal limits. She is not pregnant and has no active bleeding.

data_table.Presentation: Right lower limb proximal DVT unprovoked; commenced apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD
data_table.Obstetric and vascular history: Two second trimester foetal losses (22 and 24 weeks); one TIA at age 32; livedo reticularis
data_table.Thrombophilia screen: Lupus anticoagulant positive on dRVVT with confirmed mixing test; anti-cardiolipin IgG 68 GPL (below 40); anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I IgG 92 units (below 20)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate change to anticoagulation?

options.text: Cease anticoagulation after 3 months on apixaban as this is now a fully treated unprovoked DVT
options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome mandates indefinite anticoagulation given recurrence risk; ceasing after 3 months contradicts the unprovoked-plus-APS profile that carries a very high recurrence rate (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline).

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily indefinitely as maintenance anticoagulation for the DVT
options.rationale: DOACs are inferior to warfarin in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome; ongoing DOAC exposes the patient to a higher recurrent thrombosis risk, particularly arterial events (Source: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

options.text: Continue apixaban and add aspirin 100 mg orally daily as combination antiplatelet-anticoagulant therapy
options.rationale: Adding aspirin to a DOAC in APS increases bleeding without matching warfarin efficacy; combination therapy is not a substitute for switching to a vitamin K antagonist (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline).

options.text: Switch apixaban to rivaroxaban 20 mg orally daily as alternative DOAC maintenance for the DVT
options.rationale: Switching between DOACs does not address the class-level failure of factor Xa inhibitors in triple-positive APS demonstrated in TRAPS; the patient still needs a vitamin K antagonist (Source: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

options.text: Cease apixaban, bridge with enoxaparin, and transition to warfarin targeting INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0)
options.rationale: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant plus anti-cardiolipin plus anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I) has a higher rate of thrombosis on DOAC than on warfarin in the TRAPS and other trials; the AU HSANZ and ISTH consensus recommends switching from DOAC to warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline; ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is a clinical and laboratory diagnosis: at least one clinical criterion (arterial, venous, or small-vessel thrombosis, or defined pregnancy morbidity) plus persistent laboratory positivity (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin IgG or IgM, or anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I IgG or IgM) at least 12 weeks apart. Triple-positive APS (all three antibodies positive) has the highest thrombotic risk. Warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) is the anticoagulant of choice; the TRAPS trial and subsequent evidence show DOACs are inferior in triple-positive APS with higher arterial event rates. Duration of anticoagulation is indefinite for a defined APS diagnosis after a thrombotic event.
key_points: Triple-positive APS: lupus anticoagulant + anti-cardiolipin + anti-beta 2 GPI
DOACs are inferior to warfarin in triple-positive APS
Target INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) on warfarin
Indefinite anticoagulation after a thrombotic event
Confirmatory antibody testing at 12 weeks
explanation.pearls: The confirmatory laboratory diagnosis of APS requires persistent antibody positivity 12 weeks apart because a single transiently positive result may be reactive (recent infection, medications, or acute thrombosis itself); triple positivity carries roughly a 10-fold recurrence risk over single positivity and is what has driven the warfarin-only recommendation in recent guidance.

sources.label: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

subtopic_detail: Sequencing management of severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the ED seeing a 64 year old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m2) who has taken his usual perindopril 8 mg orally and spironolactone 25 mg orally this morning, and has attended for a routine review with 2 days of diarrhoea and reduced oral intake. He does not describe chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.

His pulse is 58 and irregular, blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate is 18, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 36.6 degrees Celsius. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 7.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), bicarbonate is 16 mmol/L (22 to 32), and creatinine is 386 micromol/L (baseline 260). Venous blood gas confirms pH 7.28.

ECG shows tall peaked T waves in V2 to V5, PR prolongation to 220 ms, and a QRS duration of 128 ms. A repeat sample sent immediately by a different route confirms potassium 7.4 mmol/L. He has two wide-bore IV cannulae in situ.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58 and irregular, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 138, potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), bicarbonate 16, creatinine 386 micromol/L (baseline 260), pH 7.28
data_table.ECG: Peaked T waves V2 to V5, PR 220 ms, QRS 128 ms

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Salbutamol 10 mg by nebuliser over 10 minutes as the sole potassium-lowering therapy today
options.rationale: Salbutamol is an adjunct shifting agent (0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L reduction) that acts over 30 minutes; it is not sufficient monotherapy for a potassium of 7.4 with QRS widening (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Actrapid insulin 10 unit IV mixed in 50 mL of 50 percent glucose over 15 minutes total
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose is essential but is a shifting step that acts over 15 to 30 minutes; myocardial stabilisation with IV calcium must come first when the QRS is widening (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV over 2 to 3 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Severe hyperkalaemia with QRS widening and PR prolongation requires immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation with IV calcium, which works within 1 to 3 minutes; insulin-dextrose and salbutamol drive intracellular shift and definitive removal comes from dialysis, but calcium is the first step (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline).

options.text: Refer for urgent haemodialysis without any medical bridging therapy before dialysis starts
options.rationale: Dialysis is the definitive potassium removal but cannot be delivered fast enough to prevent asystole from a widening QRS; medical bridging with calcium and insulin-dextrose is mandatory during vascular access and dialysis initiation (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline).

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally as a single dose with no other medical intervention
options.rationale: Potassium binders act over hours to remove potassium and have no acute role in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; immediate cardiac protection with IV calcium is first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any potassium with ECG changes) requires immediate sequenced management. Step one is myocardial membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes (or IV calcium chloride 10 percent 5 mL through a central line), acting within 1 to 3 minutes to prevent arrhythmia. Step two is intracellular potassium shift with IV actrapid insulin 10 unit in 50 mL 50 percent glucose over 15 minutes, and nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg as an adjunct. Step three is definitive removal (dialysis, potassium binder, or reversal of the precipitating drug or condition). Withdrawal of the ACE inhibitor and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is essential.
key_points: Sequence: stabilise, shift, then remove
IV calcium is the first step when ECG changes are present
Insulin-dextrose gives shift over 15 to 30 minutes
Salbutamol nebulised is an adjunct shifting agent
Dialysis is the definitive removal for renal failure
explanation.pearls: The QRS widening of hyperkalaemia represents the loss of the rapid depolarisation phase and heralds imminent sine-wave morphology and asystole within minutes; IV calcium is the only intervention that acts on that timescale, and it can be safely repeated at 5 to 10 minute intervals until ECG normalisation while insulin and definitive removal are being organised.

subtopic_detail: Volume assessment discriminating SIADH from hypovolaemic hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78 year old man admitted with community-acquired pneumonia 3 days ago, initially treated with IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, transitioned to oral amoxicillin plus doxycycline yesterday. His pneumonia is clinically improving.

Today he is asymptomatic from a neurological perspective and orientated. His pulse is 78, blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate is 18, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 36.6 degrees Celsius. Mucous membranes are moist, capillary refill is under 2 seconds, JVP is 3 cm above the sternal angle, and there is no peripheral oedema.

Sodium is 122 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium is 4.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), urea is 3.4 mmol/L (2.5 to 8.0), creatinine is 74 micromol/L (60 to 110), and glucose is 5.2 mmol/L. Serum osmolality is 258 mOsm/kg (275 to 295). Urine osmolality on a spot sample is 462 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 48 mmol/L. TSH is 1.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and 8 am cortisol is 480 nmol/L (140 to 600). He is on no medication known to cause SIADH other than the amoxicillin.

data_table.Volume status: Pulse 78, BP 128/78 mmHg with no postural drop, JVP 3 cm above sternal angle, moist mucous membranes, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 122, potassium 4.0, urea 3.4, creatinine 74, glucose 5.2 mmol/L
data_table.Osmolality: Serum 258 mOsm/kg (275 to 295); urine 462 mOsm/kg; urine sodium 48 mmol/L; TSH 1.4, cortisol 480 nmol/L (140 to 600)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Commence demeclocycline 300 mg orally twice daily for pharmacological aquaresis
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is second-line for chronic SIADH refractory to fluid restriction and carries nephrotoxicity risk; first-line management of asymptomatic SIADH is fluid restriction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1000 mL IV over 6 hours as volume resuscitation
options.rationale: Giving isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because free water is retained while sodium is excreted; isotonic saline is only appropriate in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which is not present here (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

options.text: Commence hypertonic 3 percent sodium chloride 150 mL IV bolus and repeat as needed
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, altered consciousness) or profound acute drops; the patient here is asymptomatic and hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination if the sodium is corrected too rapidly (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

options.text: Restrict fluid intake to under 800 mL per 24 hours and reassess sodium at 24 hours
options.rationale: The euvolaemic patient with hypotonic hyponatraemia, urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg (in this case 462), and urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal axes, meets criteria for SIADH; fluid restriction to under 1 litre daily is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Commence tolvaptan 15 mg orally daily as vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is reserved for SIADH refractory to fluid restriction, has PBS restrictions in Australia, and carries risks of overly rapid correction and hepatotoxicity requiring inpatient initiation; it is not first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: The diagnostic algorithm for hyponatraemia proceeds through three questions: is the plasma osmolality low (true hypotonic hyponatraemia), what is the urine osmolality, and what is the volume status. Hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg indicates inappropriate ADH activity. Adding a euvolaemic volume status and a urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, in the absence of thyroid or adrenal insufficiency, defines SIADH. Common causes include central nervous system pathology, pulmonary disease (pneumonia), malignancy (especially small cell lung cancer), and drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, chemotherapy agents). Management begins with fluid restriction under 1 litre per day for asymptomatic patients; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100
Urine sodium over 30 mmol/L supports SIADH over hypovolaemia
Fluid restriction under 1 litre is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH
Hypertonic saline for severe symptoms only
Correct at maximum 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid demyelination
explanation.pearls: The KHA-CARI correction cap is 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (6 mmol/L in chronic hyponatraemia with high demyelination risk), and if you overshoot the AU rescue is 5 percent dextrose plus desmopressin to re-lower the sodium and then correct at a controlled rate over the next 24 hours.

subtopic_detail: Biologic escalation timing in an acute ulcerative colitis flare
stem:
You are the gastroenterology advanced trainee reviewing a 32 year old woman with ulcerative colitis on the ward on day 4 of admission for an acute severe flare (Truelove and Witts criteria met: 12 bloody stools daily, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, pulse 108, haemoglobin 106 g/L, CRP 82 mg/L at admission). She was commenced on IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly on admission.

Today her stool frequency is 8 bloody stools in 24 hours, CRP has fallen from 82 to 48 mg/L, and albumin is 28 g/L (35 to 50). Her pulse is 92, blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate is 16, SpO2 is 98 percent on room air, and temperature is 37.4 degrees Celsius. Abdominal examination is soft with generalised tenderness but no peritonism, and the abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation (transverse colon 5.2 cm).

Infective screen including stool culture, C. difficile PCR, cytomegalovirus PCR on biopsies from admission flexible sigmoidoscopy, and blood cultures are all negative. She has been reviewed by colorectal surgery who are aware of the case. Her thiopurine methyltransferase activity is normal, and hepatitis B and TB screens are negative.

data_table.Admission severity (Truelove and Witts): 12 bloody stools/day, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, pulse 108, haemoglobin 106 g/L, CRP 82 mg/L
data_table.Day 4 response: 8 bloody stools/24 hours; CRP 48 mg/L; albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50); pulse 92, BP 118/72, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Stool culture, C. difficile PCR, CMV PCR on biopsy, blood cultures negative; transverse colon 5.2 cm on AXR; TPMT normal; hepatitis B and TB screens negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in medical therapy?

options.text: Commence oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg orally daily while continuing IV hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Thiopurines have onset over 8 to 12 weeks and are useful for maintenance not rescue; they have no role in acute severe steroid-refractory disease as monotherapy (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Continue IV hydrocortisone at 100 mg six-hourly for a further 5 days without changing the regimen
options.rationale: Continuing IV steroids beyond the day 3 to 5 assessment window when Travis criteria are met delays effective rescue therapy and increases the risk of complications including colonic dilatation and perforation (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Refer for urgent subtotal colectomy without a trial of rescue medical therapy
options.rationale: Immediate colectomy is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage, toxic megacolon (over 5.5 cm with systemic toxicity), or failure of a documented rescue therapy trial; rescue medical therapy is offered first (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Commence infliximab 5 mg/kg IV as an induction dose and reassess response in 72 hours
options.rationale: The Oxford Travis criteria (over 8 stools per day, or 3 to 8 stools per day plus CRP over 45 mg/L at day 3 of IV steroid) identify steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis; rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is indicated before colectomy is considered, with reassessment at 72 hours (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg orally daily as a step-down from IV hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Step-down to oral steroid is appropriate when IV therapy has produced clinical response, not when the patient meets Travis criteria for steroid-refractory disease; escalating not stepping down is required here (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by Truelove and Witts criteria (at least 6 bloody stools per day plus one of pulse over 90, temperature over 37.8, haemoglobin under 105 g/L, ESR over 30, or CRP over 30) and is managed with admission for IV corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly). Response is assessed at day 3 to 5 using the Oxford Travis criteria: over 8 bloody stools per day, or 3 to 8 bloody stools per day with CRP over 45 mg/L, identifies steroid-refractory disease requiring rescue therapy. Rescue options are infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day IV. Reassessment at 72 hours after rescue selects patients for colectomy if there is no response. Immediate surgery is reserved for perforation, haemorrhage, or toxic megacolon.
key_points: Truelove and Witts: acute severe UC diagnosis
Oxford Travis criteria at day 3 to 5: steroid-refractory
Rescue with infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin
Reassess response at 72 hours after rescue
Colectomy for perforation, haemorrhage, toxic megacolon or rescue failure
explanation.pearls: Travis criteria at day 3 predict a colectomy risk of around 85 percent without rescue therapy and around 30 percent with infliximab or ciclosporin rescue, which is why day 3 assessment is the pivot point in the AU pathway and delays beyond it are strongly associated with worse outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Fluid resuscitation targets in acute pancreatitis
stem:
You are the surgical registrar on the acute care ward at 04:00 admitting a 58 year old woman with 8 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting. Ultrasound in the ED confirmed gallstones without common bile duct dilatation. Serum lipase is 1840 unit/L (below 60) and there is no ascending cholangitis (no fever, no jaundice, alkaline phosphatase within normal limits).

Her pulse is 108, blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate is 20, SpO2 is 96 percent on room air, and temperature is 37.4 degrees Celsius. Weight is 72 kg. Sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), urea is 8.4 mmol/L (2.5 to 8.0), creatinine is 102 micromol/L (60 to 110), haematocrit is 0.46 (0.36 to 0.46), CRP is 68 mg/L (below 5), and lactate is 2.4 mmol/L (below 2.0). Glucose is 8.2 mmol/L.

She has no chronic kidney or heart disease and is on no regular medication. Urine output over the last 4 hours has been 30 mL total. Bedside abdominal examination shows generalised tenderness without peritonism and no palpable mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 138, urea 8.4, creatinine 102, haematocrit 0.46 (0.36 to 0.46), CRP 68 mg/L (below 5), lactate 2.4, glucose 8.2 mmol/L
data_table.Urine output: 30 mL over the last 4 hours (about 0.1 mL/kg/hour)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Hartmann's solution at 200 to 250 mL per hour IV titrated to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour
options.rationale: The 2022 WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance moved from aggressive to moderate goal-directed fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis; a Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte rate of 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit reduces fluid overload without worsening pancreatitis outcomes (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline; WATERFALL trial; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Aggressive Hartmann's resuscitation with 10 mL/kg IV bolus then 3 mL/kg/hour over 48 hours
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid resuscitation was standard until 2022 but WATERFALL and subsequent trials showed higher fluid overload and worse outcomes without pancreatitis benefit; the AU guidance shifted to moderate goal-directed fluid rates (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL per hour IV with no lactate-based balanced fluid used
options.rationale: Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) are preferred over 0.9 percent sodium chloride in acute pancreatitis because saline resuscitation worsens hyperchloraemic acidosis without any pancreatitis-specific benefit (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Restrict IV maintenance fluid to 50 mL per hour and rely on oral intake for volume repletion
options.rationale: Restrictive fluid strategy in a patient with a urine output of 30 mL over 4 hours and elevated haematocrit and urea perpetuates hypovolaemia and drives acute kidney injury; goal-directed rather than restrictive is the current standard (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Human albumin 4 percent 500 mL IV boluses repeated to CVP target above 12 mmHg on monitoring
options.rationale: Colloid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has no evidence of benefit over balanced crystalloid, is significantly more expensive, and CVP-guided resuscitation is not recommended in current AU practice for acute pancreatitis (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

explanation.summary: Fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has shifted from aggressive (10 mL/kg bolus and 3 mL/kg/hour for 48 hours) to moderate goal-directed strategy based on the WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance. A balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) at 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour, haematocrit trend, and improvement in urea and lactate is now standard. The change reflects consistent findings of fluid overload harm (acute respiratory distress syndrome, abdominal compartment syndrome, and multiorgan failure) without a mortality benefit from aggressive resuscitation. Analgesia (usually IV opioid), early oral or nasojejunal nutrition, and treatment of the underlying cause (early ERCP for cholangitis, laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the same admission for gallstone pancreatitis) round out the pathway.
key_points: Moderate goal-directed replaces aggressive resuscitation in AU practice
Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte at 200 to 250 mL/hour is standard
Titrate to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit trend
Aggressive resuscitation causes ARDS and abdominal compartment syndrome
Early cholecystectomy on same admission for gallstone pancreatitis
explanation.pearls: The WATERFALL trial stopped early for harm in the aggressive resuscitation arm, driven by fluid overload without a pancreatitis benefit, which is why the AU HPB Society guidance now caps first-24-hour fluid volume at around 5 litres for most adults rather than the previous 6 to 8 litre targets.

subtopic_detail: Perioperative bridging in a patient on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve
stem:
You are the perioperative medicine registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with a mechanical mitral valve (bileaflet) implanted 8 years ago for rheumatic disease. She takes warfarin 5 mg orally each night with a target INR of 2.5 to 3.5 (mechanical mitral) and her INR has been stable in range on this dose for the last 12 months.

She is scheduled for elective right hemicolectomy for a T1 colorectal adenocarcinoma in 8 days. She has no active bleeding, no personal history of thrombosis on warfarin, and no prior stroke. Her creatinine is 82 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR is over 60, platelets are 240 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin is 128 g/L (115 to 165). Her weight is 76 kg.

The colorectal surgeon has requested written perioperative anticoagulation instructions. The anaesthetist plans neuraxial anaesthesia is not required, and the case is scheduled as the first on the morning list. She is willing to attend daily for INR checks in the week prior to surgery and is prepared to self-inject twice daily if instructed.

data_table.Anticoagulation indication: Mechanical mitral valve (bileaflet) 8 years, target INR 2.5 to 3.5
data_table.Baseline labs: Creatinine 82 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR over 60, platelets 240 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L
data_table.Surgery: Elective right hemicolectomy for T1 adenocarcinoma in 8 days

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate perioperative anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch warfarin to apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily starting day minus 5 as alternative anticoagulant
options.rationale: DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves after the RE-ALIGN trial showed increased thrombosis and bleeding on dabigatran versus warfarin; apixaban has no TGA indication for mechanical valves (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Continue warfarin at 5 mg nightly through surgery aiming for an INR of about 2.0 on operation day
options.rationale: An intra-operative INR of 2.0 is unsafe for laparotomy and hemicolectomy; continuing warfarin through surgery is only appropriate for minor procedures with predictable haemostasis (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 5 with no bridging heparin and resume warfarin on the evening after surgery
options.rationale: No bridging in a mechanical mitral valve leaves a high-risk patient unprotected during the 10 to 14 day period of subtherapeutic INR around surgery; the AU standard is therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 5, start therapeutic enoxaparin day minus 3, omit morning dose, resume post-op
options.rationale: A mechanical mitral valve is a high thromboembolic risk category (annualised risk over 10 percent) and mandates therapeutic-dose bridging with low molecular weight heparin around perioperative warfarin interruption; the ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis and ACC 2017 update place this patient in the group where bridging benefit outweighs bleeding harm (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline; ACC 2017 Perioperative Anticoagulation Update).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 3 and commence prophylactic-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously as bridge
options.rationale: Prophylactic-dose LMWH does not provide thromboembolic protection for a high-risk mechanical mitral valve; therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily is required in this indication (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

explanation.summary: Perioperative anticoagulation planning stratifies patients by thromboembolic risk (annualised) and bleeding risk of the procedure. Mechanical mitral valves fall into the high-risk category with annualised thromboembolic risk over 10 percent, and warfarin interruption for surgery mandates therapeutic-dose low molecular weight heparin bridging (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily). Warfarin is stopped 5 days pre-op, LMWH is started when INR falls under 2, the last therapeutic-dose LMWH is 24 hours before surgery (12 hours for prophylactic dose), and warfarin is resumed the evening of surgery with LMWH continued until INR is therapeutic. Low-risk atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VA of 3 or below and no prior stroke does not require bridging.
key_points: Mechanical mitral valve is high thromboembolic risk (over 10% annualised)
Therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging required around warfarin interruption
Last therapeutic LMWH 24 hours before surgery
DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves
Low-risk AF with CHA2DS2-VA 3 or below does not require bridging
explanation.pearls: The BRIDGE trial found that low-risk AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 3 or below) does not benefit from bridging and suffers more bleeding, but the same trial excluded mechanical valves and rheumatic mitral disease; those two groups remain the residual indication for therapeutic bridging in current AU perioperative guidance.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

subtopic_detail: Mode of delivery counselling after prior third or fourth degree perineal tear
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a birth planning clinic seeing a 32 year old woman at 34 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first birth 2 years ago was a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3800 g baby complicated by a 4a perineal tear (external anal sphincter over 50 percent thickness torn, internal anal sphincter intact) that was repaired by an experienced consultant obstetrician in theatre with an appropriate follow-up pathway.

Since the first birth she reports rare flatus incontinence around 2 to 3 times per month but no faecal incontinence or urgency, no dyspareunia, and no perineal pain. An endoanal ultrasound at 6 weeks postpartum from the first birth showed a healed but attenuated external anal sphincter defect at the 12 o'clock position spanning around 60 degrees. Anal manometry at 12 weeks postpartum showed a resting sphincter pressure of 42 mmHg (over 40) and squeeze pressure of 96 mmHg (over 60).

This pregnancy is uncomplicated. Foetal biometry today shows an estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile at 34 weeks, cephalic presentation, and anterior placenta. She asks for advice on mode of delivery in this pregnancy.

data_table.Previous obstetric history: Prior spontaneous vaginal delivery with 4a tear repaired in theatre by consultant obstetrician
data_table.Continence and imaging: Rare flatus incontinence 2 to 3 per month; no faecal incontinence or urgency; endoanal US showed healed sphincter with 60 degree defect at 12 o'clock; anal manometry resting 42 mmHg and squeeze 96 mmHg
data_table.Current pregnancy: 34 weeks; EFW 55th centile; cephalic; anterior placenta

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate recommendation for mode of delivery counselling?

options.text: Support planned vaginal birth after discussing recurrent tear risk with continence review in third trimester
options.rationale: RANZCOG and RCOG guidance recommends offering planned vaginal birth to women with prior third or fourth degree tear who are asymptomatic (or with only minor flatus incontinence) and have normal or adequate anal manometry, because absolute recurrent tear risk is around 5 to 7 percent, most women retain continence after a further vaginal birth, and elective caesarean carries its own morbidity and future pregnancy implications (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG; RCOG Green-top Guideline 29).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend planned elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the default subsequent mode of delivery
options.rationale: Elective caesarean is offered to women with significant faecal incontinence or urgency or symptomatic sphincter defect; it is not the default for an asymptomatic woman with preserved manometry, given the maternal morbidity and future-pregnancy implications (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend planned vaginal birth with prophylactic mediolateral episiotomy at all subsequent vaginal births
options.rationale: Routine mediolateral episiotomy has not been shown to reduce recurrent third or fourth degree tear risk in RCTs and is not the RANZCOG recommendation for women with prior tears; the decision on episiotomy is individualised (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Recommend induction of labour at 38 weeks to limit foetal size and reduce risk of recurrent perineal tear
options.rationale: Induction of labour for the sole purpose of limiting foetal size and reducing tear risk in this indication is not supported by RCT evidence and has separate maternal and neonatal implications; it is not the RANZCOG recommendation (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

options.text: Defer any decision on mode of delivery until labour has commenced and foetal size is confirmed on admission
options.rationale: Antenatal counselling and shared decision-making on mode of delivery is a RANZCOG standard for women with prior significant perineal trauma; deferring the discussion until labour commences forgoes the opportunity for informed choice (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG

explanation.summary: Women with a prior third or fourth degree perineal tear (obstetric anal sphincter injury or OASI) are counselled antenatally on mode of delivery for subsequent pregnancies. RANZCOG guidance supports offering planned vaginal birth to women who are asymptomatic (or with only minor flatus incontinence) and have normal or adequate anal manometry, because the absolute recurrent tear risk is around 5 to 7 percent and most retain continence. Elective caesarean section is offered to women with significant faecal incontinence or urgency, symptomatic sphincter defect, or a strong preference to avoid recurrent perineal trauma. Assessment includes symptom review, anal manometry, and endoanal ultrasound where available. Routine mediolateral episiotomy in subsequent vaginal birth is not evidence-based for this indication and remains an individualised decision.
key_points: OASI prior tear: mode of delivery counselling in subsequent pregnancy
Asymptomatic with preserved manometry: offer planned vaginal birth
Elective caesarean for symptomatic incontinence or urgency
Recurrent tear risk around 5 to 7 percent overall
Routine prophylactic episiotomy not evidence-based
explanation.pearls: Anal manometry after OASI is the pivotal continence test in the RANZCOG algorithm because it discriminates functional sphincter reserve better than sonographic defect size alone; a preserved squeeze pressure above 60 mmHg with only minor flatus incontinence predicts a low probability of decompensation after a second vaginal birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Tear CPG
